subtopic_detail: Bronchiolitis oxygen escalation from low-flow nasal prongs
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 5 month old girl on the ward at 02:00 with her second night of bronchiolitis. She was born at 38 weeks and has no chronic medical problems. Nasopharyngeal swab confirms respiratory syncytial virus.

She was started on low-flow nasal prong oxygen at 1 L per minute two hours ago for oxygen saturations of 88 percent. Her mother has been feeding her small volumes by bottle every two hours which she is tolerating without vomiting. On assessment she has pulse rate 168 per minute, respiratory rate 62 per minute, oxygen saturation 91 percent, temperature 37.8 degC. She has moderate subcostal and intercostal recession, nasal flaring and audible wheeze; there is no head bobbing or grunting. Chest auscultation reveals widespread fine crackles and expiratory wheeze bilaterally, air entry symmetrical. She is alert, tracking her mother and settling with a dummy between assessments.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 168 /min, respiratory rate 62 /min, SpO2 91% on nasal prong O2 1 L/min, temperature 37.8 degC
data_table.Work of breathing: Moderate subcostal and intercostal recession, nasal flaring, no grunting, no head bobbing
data_table.Chest examination: Bilateral fine inspiratory crackles and expiratory wheeze, symmetrical air entry
data_table.Feeding: Bottle feeds every 2 hours tolerated without vomiting
data_table.History: 5 months, born 38 weeks, no comorbidity, RSV positive, second night of illness

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in oxygen and respiratory support?

options.text: Increase low-flow nasal prong oxygen up to 2 L per minute and reassess work of breathing and saturation after a further one hour period on this titrated flow
options.rationale: Low-flow nasal prong oxygen up to 2 L/min is the first-line escalation for bronchiolitis; reassessment before moving to high-flow is required. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Start high-flow humidified nasal cannula oxygen at 2 L per kilogram per minute with fraction of inspired oxygen 0.4 and reassess work of breathing after one hour
options.rationale: High-flow nasal cannula is reserved for failure of low-flow therapy (persistent desaturation or worsening work of breathing at 2 L/min); premature escalation is not supported. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Start continuous positive airway pressure via mask at 6 cmH2O with fraction of inspired oxygen 0.35 and admit to the paediatric intensive care unit for closer respiratory monitoring
options.rationale: CPAP is reserved for severe bronchiolitis with impending failure (grunting, apnoea, exhaustion, HFNC failure); not indicated at this severity. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Give nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg in oxygen and reassess work of breathing and oxygenation at 20 minutes before deciding on further oxygen escalation for this patient
options.rationale: Bronchodilators are not recommended in bronchiolitis under 12 months; salbutamol has no benefit and may worsen ventilation-perfusion mismatch. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Continue current nasal prong oxygen at 1 L per minute and add nebulised 3 percent hypertonic saline every four hours to reduce airway secretions and improve mucus clearance
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is not routinely recommended in Australian bronchiolitis pathways; escalation of oxygen is the priority when saturations remain below 92 percent. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Bronchiolitis is a clinical diagnosis in children under 12 months with viral upper respiratory prodrome progressing to wheeze, crackles and increased work of breathing. RCH guidance targets oxygen saturation 90 percent or greater. Low-flow nasal prong oxygen (up to 2 L/min) is first line when supplemental oxygen is needed. High-flow humidified nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min is escalation after failure of low-flow for at least one to two hours. Bronchodilators, adrenaline, steroids, hypertonic saline and chest physiotherapy are not routinely indicated in bronchiolitis. Feeding via nasogastric tube or intravenous fluid at two-thirds maintenance is used when oral intake falls below 50 percent.
key_points: Oxygen target in bronchiolitis is SpO2 at or above 90 percent (RCH).
Low-flow nasal prong oxygen up to 2 L/min is first-line escalation before HFNC.
Salbutamol, adrenaline, steroids, hypertonic saline are not recommended routinely.
explanation.pearls: Titrate low-flow nasal prong oxygen up to 2 L/min in bronchiolitis before escalating to high-flow; SpO2 target is 90 percent or greater at RCH.

subtopic_detail: Dexamethasone dose selection in moderate croup at emergency department presentation
stem:
You are the paediatric emergency registrar assessing a 2 year old boy brought in by his father at 22:00 with a barking cough and noisy breathing that started this evening. He has had a runny nose and low-grade fever for two days. He is otherwise well with no asthma and no previous intubation.

At triage he was sitting on his father's knee. Ten minutes later on your review he has pulse rate 132 per minute, respiratory rate 34 per minute, oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air, temperature 37.9 degC. There is audible inspiratory stridor at rest which resolves when he settles. Suprasternal recession is present. He is drinking sips of water and answering his father in short phrases. There is no drooling and no cyanosis. On auscultation chest is clear. Total Westley croup score is 4.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 132 /min, respiratory rate 34 /min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 37.9 degC
data_table.Airway examination: Inspiratory stridor at rest which resolves at rest with settling, suprasternal recession, no drooling, no cyanosis
data_table.Chest examination: Auscultation clear bilaterally, no crackles or wheeze
data_table.History: 2 years, well child, 2-day URTI prodrome, barking cough tonight

lead_in: Which oral steroid dose is most appropriate now?

options.text: Oral prednisolone 1 mg per kilogram single dose and observe for thirty minutes on the short-stay unit before considering discharge home once stridor at rest has fully resolved
options.rationale: Prednisolone 1 mg/kg is inferior to dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg in croup due to shorter half-life and higher relapse rate; RCH prefers dexamethasone. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg per kilogram single dose and observe on the short-stay unit for a minimum of thirty minutes before considering discharge home under written parent handout
options.rationale: 0.6 mg/kg is the higher dose reserved for severe croup or those receiving nebulised adrenaline; not required for moderate croup. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000 immediately and dexamethasone 0.6 mg per kilogram orally, then observe for three hours minimum before considering discharge home
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline is reserved for severe croup (stridor at rest with marked respiratory distress) or failure of steroid; not indicated when stridor settles at rest. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Nebulised budesonide 2 mg single dose and discharge with a written croup handout after thirty minutes of observation on the short-stay unit if stridor is settled at rest
options.rationale: Nebulised budesonide is a second-line option when oral dexamethasone cannot be tolerated; oral dexamethasone is preferred first line. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg per kilogram single dose and observe on the short-stay unit for a minimum of thirty minutes before considering discharge home under written parent handout
options.rationale: RCH recommends dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg orally for mild or moderate croup; 0.6 mg/kg is only for severe croup. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary: Croup is a viral laryngotracheobronchitis with barking cough, hoarse voice and inspiratory stridor, typically age 6 months to 6 years. RCH severity grades on the Westley score: mild (score 0-2), moderate (3-5), severe (6-11). Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg is first line for mild and moderate croup; 0.6 mg/kg is reserved for severe croup. Nebulised adrenaline (5 mL of 1:1000 as a flat dose, not per kilogram) is used for severe croup or failure to improve; minimum three-hour observation is required after the last adrenaline dose. Nebulised budesonide 2 mg is an alternative when oral steroid cannot be tolerated.
key_points: Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg is first line for mild and moderate croup at RCH.
0.6 mg/kg dexamethasone is reserved for severe croup or with nebulised adrenaline.
Nebulised adrenaline is a flat 5 mL of 1:1000, three-hour minimum observation after.
explanation.pearls: Moderate croup at RCH gets oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg once; reserve 0.6 mg/kg and nebulised adrenaline for severe croup with stridor and marked distress at rest.

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing functional constipation from organic disease requiring investigation in a toddler
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in an outpatient clinic seeing a 20 month old boy referred by his general practitioner for constipation. He was born at 39 weeks by normal vaginal birth and passed meconium in the first 12 hours of life. He was breastfed until 12 months and now eats a varied diet with adequate fibre and water.

His mother reports one hard pellet-like stool every four to five days for the last six months, with visible straining and one episode of streaks of blood on the outside of the stool three weeks ago. There has been no soiling between stools. He has grown along the 25th centile for weight and height since birth without any drop off. He walked at 13 months and has 20 words. His abdomen is soft and non-tender with no palpable mass; the anus is normally positioned with intact anocutaneous reflex; spine and lower limbs are neurologically normal. Full blood count and coeliac serology were normal one month ago.

data_table.Bowel history: One hard pellet-like stool every 4-5 days for 6 months, straining, streak of blood 3 weeks ago, no soiling
data_table.Newborn history: Meconium passed within first 12 hours, term birth
data_table.Growth: 25th centile weight and height stable since birth
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft non-tender no mass, anus normally sited, anocutaneous reflex intact, lower limb neurology normal
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count and coeliac serology normal 1 month ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Referral for anorectal manometry and rectal suction biopsy to exclude short-segment Hirschsprung disease before starting any laxative therapy in this toddler with pellet-like stools
options.rationale: Meconium in first 24 hours, normal growth, normal exam and no failure of oral laxatives make Hirschsprung very unlikely; biopsy is not first line. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Movicol Junior oral disimpaction regimen for four days and then daily movicol maintenance titrated to soft stools with review at four weeks and parent education on toileting and diet
options.rationale: This is functional constipation (Rome IV) without red flags; RCH recommends osmotic laxative disimpaction and maintenance with behavioural advice. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Abdominal radiograph to assess faecal loading and thyroid function tests to exclude hypothyroidism as a contributing organic cause before any laxative therapy is commenced
options.rationale: Plain radiograph is not recommended for diagnosis or severity of constipation; thyroid screening not indicated without other features of hypothyroidism. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Trial of a cow milk protein exclusion diet for four weeks with soy or extensively hydrolysed formula substitution and review of stool frequency before adding any pharmacological laxative therapy
options.rationale: Cow milk protein trial is considered when standard laxative treatment has failed for 4 weeks; not first line without a trial of osmotic laxative. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Enema with sodium citrate microlax daily for one week to relieve the impaction before commencing osmotic maintenance therapy and structured toileting advice at follow-up review
options.rationale: Rectal disimpaction is reserved for oral disimpaction failure; oral macrogol (Movicol Junior) is first line and better tolerated than enemas. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

explanation.summary: Functional constipation is diagnosed by Rome IV criteria (two or more of: two or fewer defecations per week, one or more episodes of incontinence per week after toilet training, history of retentive posturing, history of painful or hard bowel movements, presence of a large faecal mass in the rectum, history of large-diameter stools that may obstruct the toilet). Red flags mandating investigation include failure to pass meconium in first 48 hours (Hirschsprung), failure to thrive, abnormal lower limb neurology or spine, palpable abdominal mass extending past umbilicus, and failure of standard laxative therapy. Management is oral osmotic disimpaction (Movicol Junior four sachets escalating over four days) then maintenance titrated to soft daily stools, with behavioural and dietary advice.
key_points: Rome IV criteria and absence of red flags define functional constipation.
Osmotic macrogol (Movicol Junior) oral disimpaction is first line; enemas rarely needed.
Meconium within 48 hours effectively excludes Hirschsprung as a cause.
explanation.pearls: Toddler with hard pellet stools, normal exam and meconium in first 24 hours is functional constipation - start Movicol Junior disimpaction then maintenance, no imaging or biopsy needed.

subtopic_detail: Recognition and treatment of incomplete Kawasaki disease in a young infant with prolonged fever
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar admitting a 9 month old girl referred by her general practitioner with fever for seven days. She has had irritability and poor feeding but no diarrhoea or rash. Her father describes bilateral red eyes without discharge and cracked lips. She has been fully immunised for age.

On examination she has pulse rate 172 per minute, respiratory rate 40 per minute, oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air, temperature 39.4 degC. There is bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection sparing the limbus, dry cracked lips with strawberry tongue, and a single 2 cm right cervical lymph node. There is no polymorphous rash and no peripheral swelling. Cardiovascular examination reveals normal heart sounds and no murmur. Investigations show C-reactive protein 148 mg/L, platelet count 620 x10^9/L, haemoglobin 96 g/L (105-140), sodium 133 mmol/L, albumin 28 g/L, ALT 78 U/L. Urinalysis shows sterile pyuria. Bedside echocardiography shows dilatation of the left anterior descending coronary artery with a z-score of 3.2.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 172 /min, respiratory rate 40 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 39.4 degC
data_table.Clinical features: Fever 7 days, bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, cracked lips with strawberry tongue, single 2 cm right cervical node, no rash, no peripheral changes
data_table.Bloods: CRP 148 mg/L, platelets 620 x10^9/L, Hb 96 g/L (105-140), Na 133 mmol/L, albumin 28 g/L, ALT 78 U/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Empirical intravenous ceftriaxone 50 mg per kilogram once daily and admit for observation of persistent fever with repeat blood cultures at 48 hours before considering any further therapy
options.rationale: Bacterial infection alone does not explain sterile pyuria plus coronary dilatation plus classical features; delaying IVIG risks coronary aneurysm. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g per kilogram single infusion with high-dose aspirin 30 mg per kilogram per day in four divided doses and admit to a paediatric cardiology-linked ward
options.rationale: Incomplete Kawasaki (4 days fever + coronary z-score >2.5 + supportive labs) meets AHA treatment criteria; IVIG plus aspirin is standard. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: High-dose oral prednisolone 2 mg per kilogram per day for two weeks then taper with oral aspirin 3 mg per kilogram per day and outpatient repeat echocardiography at six weeks
options.rationale: Adjunctive corticosteroids may be added for high-risk Kawasaki or IVIG failure; corticosteroid alone without IVIG is not first line. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Intravenous infliximab 5 mg per kilogram single infusion and continue aspirin 3 mg per kilogram per day with cardiology follow-up echocardiography scheduled at six weeks post infusion
options.rationale: Infliximab is reserved for IVIG-resistant Kawasaki (persistent fever after second IVIG); it is not first-line therapy. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 50 mg per kilogram once daily plus intravenous vancomycin 15 mg per kilogram every six hours and continued observation while awaiting blood culture results
options.rationale: Antibiotic monotherapy delays definitive treatment; the coronary z-score of 3.2 with supportive features requires immediate IVIG. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)

explanation.summary: Kawasaki disease is a self-limited medium-vessel vasculitis of childhood; the major complication is coronary artery aneurysm. Classical criteria require fever for five or more days plus four of five: bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, polymorphous rash, cervical lymphadenopathy above 1.5 cm (usually unilateral), oral mucosal changes (strawberry tongue or cracked lips), and peripheral extremity changes. Incomplete Kawasaki is diagnosed when fever plus fewer criteria is combined with supportive laboratory or echocardiographic findings: raised CRP or ESR, platelets above 450 after seven days, anaemia, raised ALT, hypoalbuminaemia, sterile pyuria, or a coronary z-score above 2.5. Treatment is intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg single infusion plus aspirin (30-50 mg/kg/day) until afebrile 48-72 hours then low-dose 3-5 mg/kg/day for 6-8 weeks.
key_points: Incomplete Kawasaki: fever plus 2-3 criteria plus supportive labs or echo (coronary z-score >2.5).
Treatment: IVIG 2 g/kg single dose plus aspirin (high then low dose).
Steroids adjunctive for high-risk; infliximab for IVIG resistance.
explanation.pearls: A febrile infant with two Kawasaki features plus raised CRP plus coronary z-score above 2.5 meets AHA criteria for incomplete Kawasaki: give IVIG 2 g/kg without waiting for classical criteria.

sources.label: AHA Scientific Statement: Diagnosis Treatment and Long-term Management of Kawasaki Disease 2017

subtopic_detail: Cyanosis with normal pulse oximetry saturation and normal arterial oxygen tension in a neonate
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar assessing a 4 week old boy brought to the emergency department by his mother because he has looked blue around the mouth intermittently for two days. He was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy and has been breastfed. He was started this week on a home-prepared vegetable puree that includes silverbeet and beetroot from his mother's vegetable garden which uses well water for irrigation.

He is alert and moving all limbs. On assessment he has pulse rate 148 per minute, respiratory rate 46 per minute, oxygen saturation 87 percent on room air, temperature 36.9 degC. There is central cyanosis of the lips and tongue that does not improve on 15 L per minute of oxygen delivered by non-rebreather mask. Cardiovascular examination reveals normal heart sounds with no murmur, femoral pulses palpable, capillary refill 2 seconds. Chest is clear on auscultation. Arterial blood gas on 15 L per minute oxygen shows pH 7.36, partial pressure of oxygen 240 mmHg, partial pressure of carbon dioxide 34 mmHg, and chocolate-brown coloured blood. Bedside echocardiography demonstrates structurally normal heart with normal outflow tracts.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 148 /min, respiratory rate 46 /min, SpO2 87% on 15 L/min non-rebreather, temperature 36.9 degC
data_table.Cardiovascular: Central cyanosis unresponsive to oxygen, normal heart sounds, no murmur, femoral pulses present, capillary refill 2 sec
data_table.Arterial blood gas: pH 7.36, PaO2 240 mmHg on 15 L/min, PaCO2 34 mmHg, chocolate-brown blood colour
data_table.Echocardiography: Structurally normal heart, normal outflow tracts
data_table.Dietary history: Home-prepared vegetable puree from well-water-irrigated garden this week

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Empirical intravenous cefotaxime 50 mg per kilogram and amoxicillin 50 mg per kilogram plus fluid resuscitation with 20 mL per kilogram normal saline for suspected neonatal sepsis
options.rationale: The picture is refractory cyanosis with normal PaO2 not septic shock; antibiotics do not address the methaemoglobin. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Cyanosis)

options.text: Commence prostaglandin E1 infusion 0.05 microgram per kilogram per minute and arrange urgent paediatric cardiology transfer for cyanotic congenital heart disease evaluation and management
options.rationale: Cyanotic congenital heart disease is excluded by structurally normal echocardiogram with normal outflow tracts; prostaglandin is not indicated. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Cyanosis)

options.text: Intravenous methylene blue 1 mg per kilogram slow infusion over five minutes and stop home-prepared vegetable puree with paediatric intensive care admission for co-oximetry monitoring
options.rationale: Chocolate-brown blood with PaO2 240 mmHg and refractory cyanosis is methaemoglobinaemia; methylene blue 1-2 mg/kg IV is the antidote. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)

options.text: Exchange transfusion with fresh whole blood via umbilical venous catheter and paediatric intensive care admission for close cardiorespiratory monitoring during and after the exchange
options.rationale: Exchange transfusion is reserved for severe methaemoglobinaemia unresponsive to methylene blue or when methylene blue is contraindicated (G6PD deficiency). (Source: TGA Poisons Information)

options.text: Intravenous ascorbic acid 100 mg every six hours for 24 hours with continued high-flow oxygen and paediatric intensive care admission for close cardiorespiratory monitoring on the ward
options.rationale: Ascorbic acid is a slow reducing agent used only when methylene blue is contraindicated; methylene blue is first line. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)

explanation.summary: Methaemoglobinaemia occurs when haem iron is oxidised from ferrous to ferric form, unable to bind oxygen and shifting the oxygen dissociation curve. In neonates, sources include high-nitrate well water used in home-prepared vegetable puree, topical anaesthetics (benzocaine, prilocaine) and dapsone. The pathognomonic finding is cyanosis with normal arterial PaO2 and chocolate-brown blood; pulse oximetry reads falsely between 82 and 88 percent. Co-oximetry measures true methaemoglobin. Treatment above 20 percent methaemoglobin or with symptoms is methylene blue 1 to 2 mg/kg IV over 5 minutes. Methylene blue is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency (haemolysis risk); ascorbic acid or exchange transfusion is the alternative.
key_points: Chocolate-brown blood with high PaO2 and refractory cyanosis is methaemoglobinaemia.
Methylene blue 1-2 mg/kg IV is first-line antidote (5-minute infusion).
Contraindicated in G6PD deficiency (haemolysis risk); use ascorbic acid instead.
explanation.pearls: A neonate with cyanosis on oxygen, PaO2 above 200 mmHg and chocolate-brown blood has methaemoglobinaemia; give methylene blue 1 mg/kg IV over 5 minutes and screen for G6PD deficiency.

subtopic_detail: Choice of induction therapy in newly diagnosed paediatric Crohn disease with terminal ileal and colonic involvement
stem:
You are the paediatric gastroenterology registrar reviewing a 14 year old boy in clinic with a two month history of colicky central abdominal pain and non-bloody diarrhoea occurring four to six times per day. He has lost 4 kilograms in two months and his height velocity has slowed with weight now on the 10th centile from a previous 50th centile.

On examination he has pulse rate 92 per minute, blood pressure 110/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degC. Abdomen is soft with mild right iliac fossa tenderness and no mass. There is one aphthous ulcer on the buccal mucosa. Perianal examination reveals no fissures or skin tags. Investigations show haemoglobin 96 g/L (120-160), platelet count 462 x10^9/L, ferritin 8 microgram/L (30-300), C-reactive protein 42 mg/L, faecal calprotectin 1200 microgram/g (below 50). Ileo-colonoscopy demonstrates aphthous ulceration and cobblestoning in the terminal ileum and patchy colitis; biopsies confirm non-caseating granulomas. Magnetic resonance enterography shows no stricture or fistula, and no perianal disease.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92 /min, blood pressure 110/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degC
data_table.Growth: Weight fallen from 50th to 10th centile over 2 months, height velocity reduced
data_table.Bloods: Hb 96 g/L (120-160), platelets 462 x10^9/L, ferritin 8 microgram/L (30-300), CRP 42 mg/L
data_table.Ileo-colonoscopy: Aphthous ulceration and cobblestoning in terminal ileum, patchy colitis, non-caseating granulomas on biopsy
data_table.MR enterography: No stricture, no fistula, no perianal disease

lead_in: What is the most appropriate induction therapy?

options.text: Induction with intravenous infliximab 5 mg per kilogram at weeks zero, two and six followed by maintenance every eight weeks and concurrent methotrexate 15 mg per square metre weekly
options.rationale: Biologic first-line induction is reserved for aggressive disease with penetrating or stricturing phenotype, perianal disease, or growth failure with prior treatment failure. (Source: ESPGHAN Paediatric Crohn Disease Guidelines 2021)

options.text: Oral prednisolone 1 mg per kilogram per day tapering weekly over eight weeks combined with azathioprine 2 mg per kilogram per day maintenance and calcium and vitamin D supplementation
options.rationale: Corticosteroids suppress linear growth in paediatric Crohn; enteral nutrition avoids this and is preferred first line for luminal disease. (Source: ESPGHAN Paediatric Crohn Disease Guidelines 2021)

options.text: Exclusive enteral nutrition with a polymeric formula as sole nutrition for six to eight weeks with staged food reintroduction and dietitian-supervised weekly weight and symptom review across the induction
options.rationale: Exclusive enteral nutrition is first-line induction in paediatric luminal Crohn without perianal or fistulising disease, equivalent to steroids for mucosal healing without growth suppression. (Source: ESPGHAN Paediatric Crohn Disease Guidelines 2021)

options.text: Induction with intravenous methylprednisolone 1 mg per kilogram twice daily for five days then switch to oral prednisolone with a rapid taper over the following four weeks
options.rationale: IV steroids are reserved for severe acute colitis with systemic upset; not indicated for stable luminal ileocolonic Crohn without severe systemic features. (Source: ESPGHAN Paediatric Crohn Disease Guidelines 2021)

options.text: Oral 5-aminosalicylate mesalazine 50 mg per kilogram per day in divided doses with folate supplementation and colonoscopy review in twelve weeks to assess mucosal response to induction
options.rationale: 5-ASA has minimal role in Crohn induction; benefit is limited to mild colonic disease and it does not induce mucosal healing here. (Source: ESPGHAN Paediatric Crohn Disease Guidelines 2021)

explanation.summary: Paediatric Crohn disease often presents with abdominal pain, diarrhoea, weight loss and growth failure. Ileocolonoscopy with biopsy plus MR enterography is standard workup. For induction of remission in luminal ileocolonic Crohn without perianal, fistulising or severe systemic disease, exclusive enteral nutrition (polymeric formula as sole nutrition for 6-8 weeks) is first line and equivalent to corticosteroids for symptom relief with superior mucosal healing and no growth suppression. Corticosteroids are reserved for EEN failure or intolerance. Anti-TNF (infliximab, adalimumab) first-line induction is reserved for aggressive phenotype (penetrating or stricturing disease, extensive small bowel disease, perianal disease, severe growth failure). Maintenance is typically azathioprine 2-2.5 mg/kg/day or methotrexate 15 mg/m2 weekly.
key_points: Exclusive enteral nutrition is first-line induction in paediatric luminal Crohn.
Steroids suppress linear growth and are second line.
First-line biologic induction is reserved for penetrating, fistulising, perianal or severe growth failure phenotypes.
explanation.pearls: Newly diagnosed paediatric Crohn with luminal ileocolonic disease and growth failure but no fistula or perianal disease gets exclusive enteral nutrition for 6-8 weeks as first-line induction, not oral steroids.

subtopic_detail: Second-line uterotonic and adjunct choice in atonic postpartum haemorrhage following syntocinon failure
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to the birthing suite for postpartum haemorrhage. A 32 year old G2P1 woman had a spontaneous vaginal birth of a 4100 gram baby 20 minutes ago following a two hour second stage. She has a history of well controlled asthma and no cardiovascular disease. Her blood pressure runs 108/68 mmHg at booking.

The placenta was delivered intact 12 minutes ago after active management with intramuscular oxytocin 10 units. Since delivery she has passed an estimated 950 mL of fresh blood into the collection drape. On assessment she has pulse rate 118 per minute, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 per minute, oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degC. The uterus is palpable at the umbilicus and boggy. Two intravenous cannulae are in place and 1 L of Hartmann solution has been running wide open. A second team member has commenced bimanual uterine massage. The perineum shows no active bleeding from tears; there is no clinical suspicion of retained placenta on inspection. Group and hold is done and cross match is pending.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118 /min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Uterine tone: Palpable at umbilicus, boggy, bimanual massage in progress
data_table.Blood loss: Approximately 950 mL fresh blood in drape 20 min post birth
data_table.Placenta: Delivered intact 12 min ago after IM oxytocin 10 units
data_table.Perineum: No active tear bleeding, no retained tissue on inspection
data_table.History: G2P1, well controlled asthma, booking BP 108/68 mmHg, no cardiovascular disease

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step for uterine atony?

options.text: Intramuscular misoprostol 800 microgram sublingual single dose alone and continued bimanual uterine massage while awaiting the cross matched blood products from the transfusion service
options.rationale: Misoprostol alone is a low-resource option; IV oxytocin infusion plus ergometrine plus TXA is the preferred multi-agent approach in a well-equipped birthing unit. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)

options.text: Intramuscular carboprost 250 microgram every fifteen minutes to a maximum of eight doses and intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g slow bolus over ten minutes with continued uterine massage
options.rationale: Carboprost is third-line uterotonic (after oxytocin and ergometrine); it is contraindicated in asthma given her history. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)

options.text: Intravenous oxytocin infusion 40 units in 1 L Hartmann over four hours plus intramuscular ergometrine 250 microgram and tranexamic acid 1 g intravenous over ten minutes
options.rationale: RANZCOG PPH pathway: after initial oxytocin bolus failure give IV oxytocin infusion plus ergometrine (BP normotensive) plus TXA within 3 hours. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)

options.text: Intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g single bolus over ten minutes only and continue bimanual uterine massage with reassessment of tone at fifteen minutes before further pharmacotherapy
options.rationale: TXA alone does not treat uterine atony; oxytocin infusion plus a second uterotonic must be given concurrently. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)

options.text: Intrauterine tamponade with a Bakri balloon inflated to 500 mL and packing of the vagina below with vaginal gauze while awaiting transfer to theatre for further definitive management
options.rationale: Balloon tamponade follows failure of pharmacological uterotonics; step up pharmacotherapy first before mechanical management. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)

explanation.summary: Postpartum haemorrhage is defined as blood loss above 500 mL after vaginal birth or 1000 mL after caesarean, or any loss causing haemodynamic compromise. Uterine atony causes 70 percent of primary PPH. The RANZCOG stepwise pharmacological approach starts with oxytocin: 5 units IV bolus or 10 units IM at delivery, then IV infusion 40 units in 1 L over 4 hours if bleeding continues. Second-line ergometrine 250 microgram IM (contraindicated in hypertension, pre-eclampsia, heart disease). Third-line carboprost 250 microgram IM every 15 minutes to maximum 2 mg (contraindicated in asthma). Fourth line misoprostol 800 microgram sublingual or rectal. Tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 hours reduces death from bleeding (WOMAN trial). Mechanical management (bimanual compression, balloon tamponade) and surgical measures follow if bleeding persists despite maximal pharmacology.
key_points: Uterotonic order: oxytocin -> ergometrine -> carboprost -> misoprostol.
Carboprost is contraindicated in asthma; ergometrine in hypertension.
Give tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 hours (WOMAN trial).
explanation.pearls: Atonic PPH after oxytocin failure and normal BP without asthma: give oxytocin infusion plus ergometrine 250 microgram IM plus tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 hours of birth.

subtopic_detail: Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection in threatened preterm birth before 30 weeks gestation
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 28 year old G3P1 woman at 28+4 weeks gestation admitted to the birth suite with regular painful contractions every 3 minutes for the last two hours. She has a history of one previous term normal vaginal birth. Her pregnancy has been low risk with normal morphology scan and midpregnancy blood pressures 110/70 mmHg.

On arrival her pulse rate is 96 per minute, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.9 degC, foetal heart rate 148 per minute on cardiotocography with normal variability and no decelerations. Speculum examination reveals clear liquor draining and a partly effaced cervix; digital examination shows cervix 3 cm dilated and 60 percent effaced. Fetal fibronectin is not done given ruptured membranes. Betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscular first dose was given ninety minutes ago and nifedipine 20 mg oral tocolysis has been started. Ultrasound at admission confirms cephalic presentation, estimated fetal weight 1200 grams (25th centile), normal liquor volume and normal Doppler indices.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96 /min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.9 degC
data_table.Speculum and vaginal exam: Clear liquor draining, cervix 3 cm dilated 60 percent effaced
data_table.Cardiotocography: Foetal heart rate 148 /min baseline, normal variability, no decelerations
data_table.Ultrasound: Cephalic, estimated fetal weight 1200 g (25th centile), normal liquor, normal Dopplers
data_table.Given so far: Betamethasone 11.4 mg IM 90 min ago, nifedipine 20 mg oral commenced

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next intervention for neuroprotection?

options.text: Intravenous betamethasone 12 mg every 12 hours for two further doses and defer any magnesium sulfate therapy until closer to imminent delivery is confirmed at less than 30 minutes
options.rationale: Betamethasone is IM, and MgSO4 should be commenced when birth is expected within 24 hours below 30 weeks (not deferred to imminent delivery). (Source: RANZCOG Antenatal Corticosteroids Statement)

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g loading over 20 minutes then 2 g per hour infusion for 12 hours only irrespective of the timing of birth with cessation at that fixed endpoint
options.rationale: The RANZCOG dose is 1 g/h maintenance (not 2 g/h) and duration is up to 24 hours or until birth; higher dose increases toxicity without benefit. (Source: RANZCOG Magnesium Sulphate for Neuroprotection Statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG Magnesium Sulphate for Neuroprotection Statement

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate 6 g loading over 20 minutes then 2 g per hour infusion for the total of 24 hours only with continued nifedipine tocolysis co-administration
options.rationale: 6 g loading is the pre-eclampsia dose, not the neuroprotection dose; combining higher MgSO4 with nifedipine risks profound hypotension. (Source: RANZCOG Magnesium Sulphate for Neuroprotection Statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG Magnesium Sulphate for Neuroprotection Statement

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g loading over 20 minutes then 1 g per hour infusion for 24 hours or until birth whichever is sooner and continue monitoring reflexes
options.rationale: MgSO4 for neuroprotection is indicated for imminent preterm birth below 30 weeks; dose is 4 g loading then 1 g/h until birth or 24 hours. (Source: RANZCOG Magnesium Sulphate for Neuroprotection Statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG Magnesium Sulphate for Neuroprotection Statement

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g single loading bolus only over 20 minutes with no ongoing infusion and reassess for further dose at 12 hours after the loading dose
options.rationale: Loading dose alone is insufficient; a maintenance infusion is required until birth or 24 hours for sustained neuroprotection. (Source: RANZCOG Magnesium Sulphate for Neuroprotection Statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG Magnesium Sulphate for Neuroprotection Statement

explanation.summary: Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection of the preterm foetus reduces the risk of cerebral palsy in babies born below 30 weeks gestation (NNT approximately 46). RANZCOG recommends offering MgSO4 when preterm birth is anticipated within 24 hours at less than 30 weeks. The neuroprotection dose is 4 g loading over 20 to 30 minutes then 1 g per hour infusion until birth or for 24 hours whichever is sooner. This is a lower maintenance dose than the pre-eclampsia protocol (4 g load then 1-2 g/h). Monitor deep tendon reflexes, respiratory rate and urine output. Calcium gluconate 1 g IV is the antidote for magnesium toxicity. Nifedipine and MgSO4 can be co-administered but blood pressure and heart rate should be monitored closely for additive hypotension.
key_points: MgSO4 neuroprotection: below 30 weeks with birth expected within 24 hours.
Dose: 4 g load over 20 min then 1 g/h until birth or 24 hours.
Monitor reflexes, RR, urine output; calcium gluconate is antidote.
explanation.pearls: Threatened preterm birth below 30 weeks gestation gets magnesium sulfate 4 g loading then 1 g/h infusion for neuroprotection - lower maintenance dose than the pre-eclampsia protocol.

sources.label: RANZCOG Magnesium Sulphate for Neuroprotection Statement

subtopic_detail: Methotrexate versus surgical management for a tubal ectopic pregnancy under the RANZCOG bhCG threshold
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 30 year old G2P0 woman referred from the emergency department with light vaginal spotting and mild right iliac fossa discomfort for two days at 7 weeks gestation by last menstrual period. She has one previous first trimester miscarriage two years ago and no other medical or surgical history.

On assessment she has pulse rate 82 per minute, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 per minute, oxygen saturation 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degC. Abdomen is soft with mild right iliac fossa tenderness and no peritonism. Speculum shows a closed cervical os and scant blood in the vault. Transvaginal ultrasound demonstrates an empty uterus with a thin decidualised endometrium (endometrial thickness 8 mm), and a 22 mm right adnexal mass separate from the ovary with a yolk sac but no foetal pole and no foetal cardiac activity. There is a trace of free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Serum beta human chorionic gonadotropin is 3800 IU/L. Full blood count, liver and renal function, and blood group are normal; she is Rhesus positive.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 82 /min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Abdominal exam: Soft, mild right iliac fossa tenderness, no peritonism
data_table.Speculum: Closed cervical os, scant blood in vault
data_table.Transvaginal ultrasound: Empty uterus (endometrium 8 mm), right adnexal mass 22 mm with yolk sac, no foetal pole, no cardiac activity, trace free fluid pouch of Douglas
data_table.Bloods: beta-hCG 3800 IU/L, FBC/LFT/UEC normal, Rhesus positive
data_table.History: G2P0, previous first-trimester miscarriage, 7 weeks by LMP

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Single-dose methotrexate 50 mg per square metre intramuscular with follow up serum beta human chorionic gonadotropin at day 4 and day 7 and weekly thereafter until non-pregnant range
options.rationale: RANZCOG criteria met: haemodynamically stable, mass <3.5 cm, no cardiac activity, bhCG <5000, no significant pain, no contraindications. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement)

options.text: Laparoscopic salpingectomy of the right fallopian tube given the haemodynamic stability and clear intact contralateral tube visualised at ultrasound with anticipated future fertility
options.rationale: Surgery is offered but not mandatory here; methotrexate is a valid alternative and preferred when RANZCOG criteria for medical management are met. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement)

options.text: Expectant management with weekly beta human chorionic gonadotropin monitoring only, no methotrexate and no surgery, awaiting spontaneous resolution over the coming weeks in outpatient clinic review
options.rationale: Expectant management is only for bhCG <1500 with declining trend and no cardiac activity on ultrasound; her level of 3800 exceeds this. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement)

options.text: Laparoscopic salpingostomy of the right fallopian tube to preserve tubal patency with intraoperative beta human chorionic gonadotropin measurement post trophoblast removal from the tube
options.rationale: Salpingostomy is offered when the contralateral tube is diseased/absent (preserve fertility); with a normal contralateral tube, salpingectomy has lower persistent trophoblast risk. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement)

options.text: Two-dose methotrexate regimen 50 mg per square metre intramuscular on day 0 and day 4 with baseline liver function tests repeated on day 7 for standard monitoring after therapy
options.rationale: Two-dose regimen is reserved for high bhCG (>5000 with normal criteria otherwise) or foetal cardiac activity; single dose is appropriate here. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement)

explanation.summary: A tubal ectopic pregnancy is confirmed by an empty uterus with an adnexal mass containing a yolk sac or foetal pole and positive serum beta-hCG. RANZCOG offers three management options based on haemodynamic status and specific criteria. Expectant management: haemodynamically stable, bhCG below 1500 with declining trend, no foetal cardiac activity. Methotrexate: haemodynamically stable, bhCG below 5000, no foetal cardiac activity, mass below 3.5 cm, no significant pain or haemorrhage, no contraindications (hepatic, renal, haematologic disease, breastfeeding), reliable follow-up. Single-dose methotrexate 50 mg/m2 IM with bhCG on days 4 and 7, expect 15 percent decline day 4 to 7. Surgical: haemodynamically unstable, ruptured, contraindications to methotrexate, or above criteria not met. Salpingectomy is preferred over salpingostomy when the contralateral tube is normal.
key_points: Methotrexate criteria: stable, bhCG below 5000, no cardiac activity, mass below 3.5 cm.
Single dose 50 mg/m2 IM with day 4 and 7 bhCG monitoring.
Salpingectomy over salpingostomy when the other tube is normal.
explanation.pearls: A stable ectopic with bhCG 3800 IU/L, no foetal cardiac activity, mass under 3.5 cm and no contraindications meets RANZCOG criteria for single-dose methotrexate 50 mg per square metre.

subtopic_detail: Recognition of HELLP syndrome without severe hypertension and immediate management priorities
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 34 year old G1P0 woman at 33+2 weeks gestation who presents at 03:00 with two days of increasing right upper quadrant pain and nausea. Booking blood pressure was 118/72 mmHg. Her pregnancy has been otherwise low risk on routine antenatal care; the 20 week morphology scan was normal.

On assessment she has pulse rate 96 per minute, blood pressure 132/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 per minute, oxygen saturation 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degC, foetal heart rate 152 per minute on cardiotocography with reduced variability but no decelerations. She is alert with mild epigastric tenderness on palpation but no rebound. Reflexes are normal. Urinalysis shows protein 2+. Investigations: haemoglobin 96 g/L (105-140), platelet count 84 x10^9/L, lactate dehydrogenase 780 U/L (120-250), aspartate aminotransferase 190 U/L (below 35), alanine aminotransferase 168 U/L, bilirubin 32 micromol/L, blood film shows schistocytes, creatinine 92 micromol/L (baseline 62), urate 0.42 mmol/L, coagulation profile within normal limits. Urine protein creatinine ratio is 128 mg per mmol. Ultrasound shows appropriate growth on the 30th centile and normal Dopplers.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96 /min, blood pressure 132/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC, FHR 152 /min
data_table.Symptoms and signs: Right upper quadrant pain 2 days, nausea, mild epigastric tenderness, reflexes normal, urine protein 2+
data_table.Bloods: Hb 96 g/L (105-140), platelets 84 x10^9/L, LDH 780 U/L (120-250), AST 190 U/L, ALT 168 U/L, bilirubin 32 micromol/L, schistocytes on film, creatinine 92 micromol/L (baseline 62), urate 0.42 mmol/L
data_table.Cardiotocography: FHR 152 baseline, reduced variability, no decelerations

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management priority?

options.text: Oral labetalol 200 mg immediate release loading dose and admit for expectant management with twice daily blood pressure and bloods aiming for spontaneous labour after 37 weeks gestation
options.rationale: HELLP with worsening bloods is not amenable to expectant management to term; delivery within 24-48 hours after steroid cover is required. (Source: RANZCOG Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline (SOMANZ))

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate loading 4 g over 20 minutes then 1 g per hour infusion with betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscular first dose and plan delivery within 24 to 48 hours
options.rationale: HELLP with organ dysfunction at 33+2 weeks warrants steroid cover for lung maturation, MgSO4 for seizure prophylaxis and expedited delivery within 24-48 hours. (Source: RANZCOG Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline (SOMANZ))

options.text: Intravenous hydralazine 5 mg bolus every 20 minutes and admit for oral nifedipine slow release 30 mg twice daily and continued monitoring with delivery planned only if blood pressure reaches 160/110
options.rationale: Her blood pressure is not in the severe range; HELLP diagnosis itself (not the BP) drives the delivery decision. (Source: RANZCOG Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline (SOMANZ))

options.text: Emergency caesarean section under general anaesthesia within one hour without steroid cover and platelet transfusion pre operatively targeting platelet count above 100 x10^9 per L
options.rationale: Immediate delivery within an hour without steroid cover misses the neonatal benefit of 24-48 hours of betamethasone; her stability allows time for both steroids and MgSO4. (Source: RANZCOG Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline (SOMANZ))

options.text: Intravenous dexamethasone 10 mg twelve hourly for HELLP-specific corticosteroid therapy and admit for expectant management with delivery planned at 37 weeks after platelet recovery
options.rationale: Dexamethasone does not improve maternal or perinatal outcomes in HELLP and does not obviate the need to deliver at this gestation. (Source: RANZCOG Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline (SOMANZ))

explanation.summary: HELLP syndrome (haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets) can occur without severe hypertension; the diagnosis is clinical and laboratory. Tennessee criteria: platelets below 100 x10^9/L, AST above 70 U/L, LDH above 600 U/L, or microangiopathic haemolysis (schistocytes, elevated bilirubin). HELLP is a severe manifestation of pre-eclampsia even if BP is not severe range. Management priorities: magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis (4 g load then 1 g/h), corticosteroids for foetal lung maturation if 24 to 34+6 weeks (betamethasone 11.4 mg IM two doses 24 hours apart), delivery within 24-48 hours regardless of gestation beyond 32-34 weeks. Antihypertensives target BP below 160/110. Dexamethasone does not improve maternal outcomes in HELLP itself but standard antenatal corticosteroid course is given for foetal lung maturation.
key_points: HELLP can occur without severe hypertension; diagnosis is haematologic and hepatic.
Deliver within 24-48 hours regardless of BP; give steroid cover if 24 to 34+6 weeks.
Give MgSO4 seizure prophylaxis; treat only severe range BP with antihypertensives.
explanation.pearls: HELLP with platelets 84 x10^9/L and AST 190 U/L at 33+2 weeks: give betamethasone for lung maturation, MgSO4 for seizure prophylaxis, plan delivery within 24-48 hours - do not manage expectantly.

subtopic_detail: Choice of surgical procedure for tubal ectopic pregnancy when the contralateral tube is absent from prior surgery
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar in theatre with your consultant to manage a 33 year old G3P0 woman with an unstable tubal ectopic pregnancy. Two years ago she had a right salpingectomy for a ruptured right tubal ectopic. She has been trying to conceive spontaneously for the past six months. She has no other medical history.

She presented tonight with acute left iliac fossa pain and fainting. On arrival she had pulse rate 132 per minute, blood pressure 88/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 per minute, oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.5 degC. She received 1 L Hartmann and 1 unit packed red cells and was transferred immediately to theatre. Serum beta human chorionic gonadotropin was 4200 IU/L. Bedside transvaginal ultrasound demonstrated a left adnexal mass 30 mm with visible yolk sac in the tube and no foetal cardiac activity, and moderate free fluid throughout the pelvis and paracolic gutters. Diagnostic laparoscopy confirms a left ampullary ectopic in the mid tube with active bleeding from the fimbriated end; the tube itself is intact with viable serosa. The right tube is absent from prior surgery. Uterus and ovaries appear healthy.

data_table.Vital signs on arrival: Pulse rate 132 /min, blood pressure 88/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.5 degC
data_table.Resuscitation: 1 L Hartmann and 1 unit packed red cells given, transferred to theatre
data_table.Transvaginal ultrasound: Left adnexal mass 30 mm with yolk sac, no foetal cardiac activity, moderate free fluid pelvis and paracolic gutters
data_table.Laparoscopic findings: Left ampullary ectopic mid tube, active bleeding from fimbriated end, tube intact and viable, right tube absent (previous salpingectomy), uterus and ovaries healthy
data_table.Fertility history: Trying to conceive 6 months, prior right salpingectomy 2 years ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate surgical procedure now?

options.text: Intraoperative methotrexate 50 mg per square metre injection into the tubal mass with tube preservation and post operative serum beta human chorionic gonadotropin monitoring to zero
options.rationale: Local methotrexate has no established role in acute haemodynamically unstable ectopic; definitive surgical removal is required. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement)

options.text: Laparoscopic salpingostomy of the left fallopian tube preserving tubal patency to allow future spontaneous conception given that the right tube is absent from the previous salpingectomy
options.rationale: Salpingostomy would preserve a tube already implicated in a recurrent ectopic; recurrent ectopic on this tube is a bigger risk than the fertility gain from preservation. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement)

options.text: Laparoscopic salpingectomy of the left fallopian tube with haemostasis and washout given the persistent trophoblast risk and higher recurrent ectopic risk in a diseased contralateral remnant
options.rationale: With a prior contralateral salpingectomy, recurrent ectopic in the only remaining tube dominates; salpingectomy has lower persistent trophoblast and recurrent ectopic than salpingostomy. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement)

options.text: Diagnostic laparoscopy only with drainage of haemoperitoneum and postoperative single dose intramuscular methotrexate for management of the ectopic tissue left in situ within the tube
options.rationale: Leaving an actively bleeding ectopic in situ risks catastrophic haemorrhage; methotrexate is contraindicated post haemoperitoneum with instability. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement)

options.text: Laparoscopic salpingectomy of the left tube plus contralateral prophylactic oophorectomy given a history of previous ipsilateral ovarian involvement in prior ectopic surgery
options.rationale: Prophylactic oophorectomy has no place in current ectopic management and would eliminate spontaneous fertility. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement)

explanation.summary: Surgical management of tubal ectopic can be salpingectomy or salpingostomy. Salpingectomy has lower persistent trophoblast rates (0 to 4 percent versus 4 to 15 percent for salpingostomy) and lower recurrent ectopic risk in the operated tube. RANZCOG recommends salpingectomy over salpingostomy when the contralateral tube is normal, because subsequent intrauterine pregnancy rates are similar and salpingectomy avoids persistent trophoblast follow-up. When the contralateral tube is diseased or absent, tube preservation via salpingostomy was traditionally recommended to preserve spontaneous fertility; however, when the affected tube is the ONLY remaining tube, recurrent ectopic risk becomes dominant. Contemporary practice weighs recurrent ectopic risk against fertility gain and, when the tube is haemodynamically unstable with significant tubal damage, salpingectomy plus assisted reproduction referral is the safer default.
key_points: Salpingectomy has lower persistent trophoblast and lower recurrent ectopic on that tube.
Prior contralateral salpingectomy: recurrent ectopic risk in the only tube dominates.
Prefer salpingectomy plus IVF referral over salpingostomy in this inversion.
explanation.pearls: Prior contralateral salpingectomy flips the classic answer: current tubal ectopic with prior right salpingectomy is treated with left salpingectomy plus IVF referral, not salpingostomy, because recurrent ectopic risk in the only tube dominates.

subtopic_detail: Decision timing for emergency caesarean during VBAC with early features of uterine scar dehiscence
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 32 year old G2P1 woman at 40+1 weeks in the birthing suite. She had a lower segment caesarean section for breech presentation two years ago and is undergoing a trial of labour after caesarean this pregnancy. Labour has been progressing normally with cervical dilatation 8 cm at last examination two hours ago on oxytocin augmentation for slow progress in first stage.

Her epidural has been effective for the last four hours. On assessment she has pulse rate 108 per minute, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 per minute, oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.9 degC, foetal heart rate 150 per minute on cardiotocography. She reports the sensation of continuous suprapubic pain breaking through her epidural in the last 20 minutes. The abdominal wall is tender between contractions. The cardiotocography shows normal baseline with reduced variability for 20 minutes and three recent late decelerations lasting up to 90 seconds with slow recovery, and a mildly tense abdomen palpable between contractions. On vaginal examination the presenting part is at spines and the cervix is 8 cm dilated.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 108 /min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.9 degC
data_table.Cardiotocography: Baseline FHR 150 /min, reduced variability 20 min, three late decelerations up to 90 sec with slow recovery
data_table.Symptoms: Continuous suprapubic pain breaking through epidural 20 min, abdomen tender between contractions
data_table.Vaginal examination: Cervix 8 cm dilated, presenting part at spines, unchanged from 2 hours ago
data_table.Augmentation: Syntocinon infusion running for slow first stage progress
data_table.History: G2P1, previous LSCS for breech 2 years ago, TOLAC this pregnancy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform amniotomy if not already done and continue augmentation for 30 minutes given the presenting part at spines and estimated fully dilated within an hour based on current progress
options.rationale: Continued augmentation with a suspected uterine scar dehiscence is contraindicated; progress projections do not override the CTG and clinical signs. (Source: RANZCOG Birth after Previous Caesarean Section Statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG Birth after Previous Caesarean Section Statement

options.text: Reduce syntocinon rate by half, position her left lateral and give 500 mL Hartmann bolus and reassess cardiotocography for further 20 minutes before deciding on operative delivery
options.rationale: Intrauterine resuscitation delays diagnosis of impending uterine rupture; the pattern is not amenable to conservative management. (Source: RANZCOG Birth after Previous Caesarean Section Statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG Birth after Previous Caesarean Section Statement

options.text: Give subcutaneous terbutaline 250 microgram for tocolysis and reposition left lateral with maternal facial oxygen and reassess cardiotocography over further 30 minutes
options.rationale: Tocolysis for suspected uterine rupture postpones definitive delivery and risks catastrophic haemorrhage; immediate caesarean is required. (Source: RANZCOG Birth after Previous Caesarean Section Statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG Birth after Previous Caesarean Section Statement

options.text: Stop syntocinon and proceed immediately to emergency caesarean section under the epidural top up for suspected uterine scar dehiscence or rupture with senior obstetric and paediatric attendance
options.rationale: New continuous pain through epidural, tender abdomen between contractions, foetal compromise on CTG in a TOLAC on oxytocin is uterine scar dehiscence until proven otherwise. (Source: RANZCOG Birth after Previous Caesarean Section Statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG Birth after Previous Caesarean Section Statement

options.text: Foetal scalp lactate sampling to quantify degree of foetal compromise and if lactate below 4.2 mmol per L continue conservative management with intrauterine resuscitation and repeat cardiotocography
options.rationale: Foetal blood sampling is contraindicated with suspected uterine rupture; the diagnosis is clinical not biochemical. (Source: RANZCOG Birth after Previous Caesarean Section Statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG Birth after Previous Caesarean Section Statement

explanation.summary: Uterine rupture in trial of labour after caesarean occurs in approximately 0.5 percent (0.7 to 0.9 percent with induction and augmentation). Warning signs include foetal heart rate abnormalities (most common - late decelerations, prolonged decelerations, foetal bradycardia), continuous abdominal pain breaking through epidural, maternal tachycardia, cessation of contractions, loss of station, vaginal bleeding, and haemodynamic instability. Diagnosis is clinical; immediate delivery by caesarean is required. Oxytocin should be stopped and delivery expedited without waiting for further evidence. Foetal scalp lactate sampling, intrauterine resuscitation and tocolysis are contraindicated as they delay definitive management. Maternal outcomes are excellent with prompt delivery; delay above 20 to 30 minutes from onset of warning signs is associated with hypoxic-ischaemic brain injury and foetal death.
key_points: Uterine rupture warning signs: FHR abnormality, continuous pain through epidural, tender abdomen.
Rupture risk 0.5 percent TOLAC baseline, higher with oxytocin augmentation.
Diagnosis is clinical; immediate emergency caesarean, no delay for FBS or resuscitation.
explanation.pearls: TOLAC with new continuous pain through epidural, tender abdomen between contractions and late decelerations on syntocinon is uterine scar dehiscence: stop syntocinon and proceed immediately to caesarean, no scalp lactate or tocolysis.

sources.label: RANZCOG Birth after Previous Caesarean Section Statement

subtopic_detail: Priorities in management of complete molar pregnancy with clinical and biochemical hyperthyroidism at diagnosis
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 29 year old G1P0 woman at 13 weeks by dates who presents with heavy vaginal bleeding for three days, tremor and one episode of vomiting per day for one week. She has no medical history and takes no regular medications. Her mother has Hashimoto thyroiditis.

On assessment she has pulse rate 128 per minute, blood pressure 148/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 per minute, oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air, temperature 37.4 degC. She has a fine tremor of the outstretched hands and warm moist palms. There is no goitre and no proptosis on eye examination. Speculum shows heavy bleeding through a partly open cervix with grape like vesicles in the vault. Uterus is enlarged to 18 weeks size on abdominal palpation. Transvaginal ultrasound demonstrates a "snowstorm" appearance filling the uterine cavity with bilateral theca lutein cysts on the ovaries and no foetal parts. Serum beta human chorionic gonadotropin is 590000 IU/L. Thyroid function: thyroid stimulating hormone below 0.01 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), free T4 32 pmol/L (10 to 20), free T3 8 pmol/L (3 to 6). Full blood count, urea and electrolytes, liver function within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 128 /min, blood pressure 148/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.4 degC
data_table.Examination: Fine tremor outstretched hands, warm moist palms, no goitre, no proptosis, uterus 18 weeks size
data_table.Speculum: Heavy bleeding through partly open cervix, grape-like vesicles in vault
data_table.Transvaginal ultrasound: Snowstorm intrauterine appearance, bilateral theca lutein cysts, no foetal parts
data_table.Bloods: beta-hCG 590000 IU/L, TSH below 0.01 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), free T4 32 pmol/L (10-20), free T3 8 pmol/L (3-6), FBC/UEC/LFT within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management step?

options.text: Total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy under general anaesthesia the same day given the biochemical hyperthyroidism and enlarged uterus at 18 weeks size
options.rationale: Hysterectomy is not routine for complete mole; suction evacuation preserves fertility and cures the hyperthyroidism. Hysterectomy is only considered in women over 40 who have completed childbearing. (Source: RANZCOG Gestational Trophoblastic Disease Statement)

options.text: Oral carbimazole 40 mg daily and defer suction dilatation and evacuation for one week until biochemical euthyroidism is achieved to reduce anaesthetic risk from thyroid storm
options.rationale: The hyperthyroidism resolves with hCG fall after evacuation, so long-course carbimazole is unnecessary and delay risks bleeding progression. (Source: RANZCOG Gestational Trophoblastic Disease Statement)

options.text: Intravenous oxytocin 40 units in 1 L Hartmann and misoprostol 400 microgram sublingual for medical evacuation to avoid surgical anaesthetic risk in the context of biochemical hyperthyroidism
options.rationale: Medical evacuation is not recommended for molar pregnancy - suction dilatation and evacuation is preferred to minimise embolisation of trophoblast to lung. (Source: RANZCOG Gestational Trophoblastic Disease Statement)

options.text: Radioactive iodine 15 mCi single dose and defer any evacuation for four weeks to allow the induced hypothyroidism to develop before considering safe surgical management
options.rationale: Radioactive iodine is contraindicated in pregnancy (including molar); it destroys the thyroid unnecessarily since hCG-mediated hyperthyroidism resolves after evacuation. (Source: RANZCOG Gestational Trophoblastic Disease Statement)

options.text: Oral propranolol 40 mg pre operatively and proceed to suction dilatation and evacuation the same day with anaesthetic and cardiology pre operative review and oxytocin infusion after evacuation is commenced
options.rationale: Molar pregnancy with hCG-mediated hyperthyroidism resolves with molar evacuation; beta blockade controls symptoms preoperatively while definitive treatment is evacuation. (Source: RANZCOG Gestational Trophoblastic Disease Statement)

explanation.summary: Complete hydatidiform mole is a gestational trophoblastic disease with grossly elevated beta-hCG that structurally resembles TSH and stimulates the TSH receptor in around 5 percent of cases, causing biochemical or clinical hyperthyroidism. Typical features are vaginal bleeding, uterus large for dates, hyperemesis, early-onset pre-eclampsia, and "snowstorm" ultrasound appearance with theca lutein cysts. Management is suction dilatation and evacuation the same day as diagnosis (medical evacuation is contraindicated due to trophoblast embolisation risk). Preoperative beta blockade with propranolol controls hyperthyroid symptoms; long-course thionamides are unnecessary because thyroid function normalises within days as hCG falls. Anti-D 625 IU IM if Rhesus negative. Post-evacuation weekly beta-hCG to non-pregnant range then monthly for six months. Contraception is essential during follow-up.
key_points: Complete mole causes hCG-mediated hyperthyroidism in around 5 percent of cases.
Suction dilatation and evacuation is first-line treatment; hyperthyroidism resolves with hCG fall.
Preoperative propranolol controls symptoms; long-course carbimazole is unnecessary.
explanation.pearls: Complete molar pregnancy with hyperthyroid features is treated by suction dilatation and evacuation the same day with preoperative propranolol - the hyperthyroidism resolves as hCG falls, so carbimazole and delay are wrong.

subtopic_detail: Recognition and initial management of lithium toxicity precipitated by an NSAID interaction
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar reviewing a 42 year old woman with bipolar I disorder brought in by her sister with one week of increasing tremor, unsteady gait and drowsiness. She has taken lithium 900 mg nocte for six years with stable serum lithium levels around 0.7 mmol/L. Two weeks ago she started ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily on a friend's advice for chronic back pain. She has no other medications.

On assessment she has pulse rate 96 per minute, blood pressure 128/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 per minute, oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degC. She is drowsy but rousable, oriented in time. Coarse tremor of the outstretched hands, hyperreflexia in the lower limbs with three beats of ankle clonus, and a broad-based ataxic gait when assisted to stand. There is no muscle rigidity and no autonomic instability. Investigations show serum lithium 1.6 mmol/L (0.6 to 1.0), creatinine 142 micromol/L (baseline 78), urea 9.2 mmol/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.6 mmol/L, thyroid stimulating hormone 3.2 mIU/L. Electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm with T wave flattening in the lateral leads. She last took her lithium 8 hours ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96 /min, blood pressure 128/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Neurology: Drowsy but rousable, oriented to time, coarse tremor outstretched hands, hyperreflexia LL, 3 beats ankle clonus, broad-based ataxic gait, no rigidity
data_table.Bloods: Lithium 1.6 mmol/L (0.6-1.0), creatinine 142 micromol/L (baseline 78), urea 9.2 mmol/L, Na 138 mmol/L, K 4.6 mmol/L, TSH 3.2 mIU/L
data_table.ECG: Sinus rhythm, T wave flattening lateral leads
data_table.Medications: Lithium 900 mg nocte (stable 6 years), ibuprofen 400 mg TDS started 2 weeks ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Whole bowel irrigation with polyethylene glycol 2 L per hour via nasogastric tube for 6 hours and admit for cardiac and neurological monitoring with 4 hourly serum lithium
options.rationale: Whole bowel irrigation is considered for acute massive ingestion of sustained-release lithium, not chronic toxicity with NSAID precipitant. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)

options.text: Continue lithium at reduced dose 450 mg nocte, stop ibuprofen and switch to paracetamol 1 g four times daily with outpatient lithium level in 3 days for reassessment
options.rationale: Chronic toxicity at 1.6 mmol/L with neurological signs mandates cessation of lithium and admission; outpatient management is unsafe. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)

options.text: Activated charcoal 50 g via nasogastric tube and admit for observation for 24 hours with 4 hourly serum lithium monitoring targeting level below 1.0 mmol/L for discharge
options.rationale: Charcoal does not bind lithium; it is ineffective. Symptomatic management with saline and dialysis consult is required. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)

options.text: Stop lithium and ibuprofen, admit for intravenous normal saline 200 mL per hour with 6 hourly serum lithium and creatinine monitoring and nephrology consult for possible haemodialysis
options.rationale: Chronic lithium toxicity with neurological features and level >1.5 needs cessation, IV fluid and dialysis consult; NSAID must be stopped as the precipitant. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)

options.text: Give sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol intravenous bolus to alkalinise the urine and increase renal lithium excretion, then admit for cardiac monitoring for 24 hours with 4 hourly levels
options.rationale: Urinary alkalinisation does not enhance lithium clearance; normal saline volume expansion and dialysis (if severe) is appropriate. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)

explanation.summary: Lithium is renally excreted; anything reducing renal function or sodium status raises lithium levels. Common precipitants of chronic toxicity: NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, thiazide diuretics, dehydration, low-salt diet, acute kidney injury. Chronic toxicity typically presents at lower levels than acute (1.2 to 2.5 mmol/L) with neurological features (coarse tremor, hyperreflexia, clonus, ataxia, dysarthria, confusion, drowsiness). Severe toxicity (above 2.5 mmol/L or severe symptoms) causes seizures, coma, arrhythmia. Management: stop lithium and precipitant, intravenous normal saline for volume expansion (aiming for good urine output), monitor lithium 4 to 6 hourly and renal function. Haemodialysis is indicated for level above 4.0 mmol/L, above 2.5 with severe symptoms, or above 2.5 with renal failure. Activated charcoal is ineffective for lithium; whole bowel irrigation is for acute massive sustained-release ingestion.
key_points: Chronic lithium toxicity is precipitated by NSAIDs, ACEi, ARBs, thiazides, dehydration.
Neurological features (tremor, clonus, ataxia, confusion) at levels above 1.2 mmol/L.
Treat with cessation, IV saline; haemodialysis for level above 4.0 or severe symptoms.
explanation.pearls: Chronic lithium toxicity at 1.6 mmol/L with neurological signs after NSAID commencement: stop lithium and ibuprofen, IV saline 200 mL/h and nephrology consult for possible dialysis.

subtopic_detail: Recognition and immediate management of serotonin syndrome from an SSRI plus tramadol co-prescription
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar reviewing a 38 year old man with generalised anxiety disorder brought in by his partner with two days of tremor, agitation and diarrhoea. He has been on sertraline 100 mg daily for six months with good response. Four days ago his general practitioner started tramadol 50 mg four times daily for acute back pain following a fall. He drinks no alcohol and takes no other medications.

On assessment he has pulse rate 128 per minute, blood pressure 158/92 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 per minute, oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air, temperature 38.4 degC. He is agitated and restless with dilated pupils, diaphoretic and flushed. There is inducible clonus at the ankles (4 beats bilaterally with spontaneous clonus in the right ankle). Hyperreflexia is more pronounced in the lower limbs than upper limbs. Muscle tone is normal in the arms and mildly increased in the legs. There is no muscle rigidity. Investigations show creatine kinase 480 U/L (below 200), urea 8.4 mmol/L, creatinine 98 micromol/L, sodium 137 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, and venous blood gas: pH 7.36, bicarbonate 22 mmol/L, lactate 2.2 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 128 /min, blood pressure 158/92 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.4 degC
data_table.Neurology: Agitated restless, dilated pupils, diaphoretic and flushed, spontaneous ankle clonus right, 4 beats induced ankle clonus bilateral, hyperreflexia LL>UL, mildly increased tone LL, no rigidity
data_table.Bloods: CK 480 U/L (<200), urea 8.4 mmol/L, creatinine 98 micromol/L, Na 137 mmol/L, K 4.2 mmol/L
data_table.Medications: Sertraline 100 mg daily 6 months, tramadol 50 mg QID started 4 days ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management step?

options.text: Give intravenous methylene blue 1 mg per kilogram as monoamine oxidase inhibitor to reduce serotonergic activity centrally and admit to intensive care for observation and monitoring
options.rationale: Methylene blue itself has serotonergic effects and would worsen the syndrome; it is contraindicated. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)

options.text: Give intramuscular bromocriptine 5 mg and intramuscular dantrolene 2 mg per kg then intubate for muscle rigidity as first-line management of neuroleptic malignant syndrome features
options.rationale: Bromocriptine and dantrolene are used for NMS not serotonin syndrome; distinguishing features are neuromuscular (clonus vs rigidity) and time course. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)

options.text: Give intramuscular haloperidol 5 mg for agitation and continue both sertraline and tramadol at reduced doses with hydration and admit for observation of the resolving syndrome
options.rationale: Continuing serotonergic agents perpetuates the syndrome; haloperidol adds anticholinergic burden without treating cause. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)

options.text: Give intravenous flumazenil 0.2 mg titrated for co-ingested benzodiazepine assumed present and continue current medications until formal drug screen is available
options.rationale: Flumazenil is not indicated (no benzodiazepine history); it can precipitate seizures. Serotonin syndrome does not need reversal - it needs cessation of the precipitants. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)

options.text: Stop sertraline and tramadol, give intravenous diazepam 5 mg titrated with active external cooling and consider oral cyproheptadine 12 mg for persistent or worsening features
options.rationale: Serotonin syndrome (Hunter criteria met: clonus, hyperthermia, hyperreflexia) after tramadol added to SSRI needs cessation, benzodiazepine, cooling; cyproheptadine for refractory cases. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)

explanation.summary: Serotonin syndrome is a clinical diagnosis with the Hunter criteria: serotonergic agent plus one of: spontaneous clonus; inducible clonus with agitation or diaphoresis; ocular clonus with agitation or diaphoresis; tremor and hyperreflexia; or hypertonia, temperature above 38 degC and ocular or inducible clonus. Common precipitants: SSRI plus tramadol, SSRI plus MAOI, SSRI plus linezolid, SSRI plus fentanyl or pethidine, SSRI plus St John wort, MDMA. Onset within hours to days. Distinguishing from NMS: serotonin syndrome features clonus and hyperreflexia predominantly in lower limbs, onset hours after precipitant; NMS features lead-pipe rigidity, onset over days after neuroleptic. Management: stop all serotonergic agents, benzodiazepines (diazepam 5-10 mg IV titrated) for agitation and tremor, active cooling for hyperthermia. Cyproheptadine (5-HT2A antagonist, 12 mg orally then 2 mg every 2 hours) for moderate to severe cases. Muscle relaxation and intubation for severe hyperthermia (above 41 degC).
key_points: Hunter criteria: serotonergic agent plus clonus/hyperreflexia/temperature.
Clonus predominantly lower limbs distinguishes from NMS rigidity.
Treat: stop precipitants, benzodiazepines, cooling, cyproheptadine if severe.
explanation.pearls: SSRI plus tramadol with fever, agitation and lower-limb clonus is serotonin syndrome: stop both agents, give diazepam 5 mg IV titrated, cool actively, add cyproheptadine 12 mg for moderate to severe cases.

subtopic_detail: Interpretation of clozapine haematological monitoring and decision to continue or interrupt therapy
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 34 year old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia on clozapine 400 mg nocte for four years in the community mental health clinic. He has been symptomatically stable on this dose with no active positive symptoms and good functional recovery, working part time. He has no other medical conditions and takes no other medications.

He is well today with no fever, no sore throat, no cough or urinary symptoms. On assessment he has pulse rate 72 per minute, blood pressure 116/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 per minute, oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degC. Cardiovascular, respiratory, abdominal and mental state examinations are unremarkable. Routine 4 weekly full blood count from yesterday shows white cell count 2.8 x10^9/L (baseline 4.5), absolute neutrophil count 1.4 x10^9/L (baseline 2.2), lymphocyte count 1.2 x10^9/L, haemoglobin 148 g/L, platelet count 240 x10^9/L, C-reactive protein below 5 mg/L.
