Two prior monthly counts have been stable at ANC 2.0 to 2.4 x10^9/L. He has no recent viral illness. Clozapine trough level 320 microgram/L (target 350 to 500) from same blood draw.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 72 /min, blood pressure 116/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.General: Well, no infective symptoms, cardiovascular/respiratory/abdominal/mental state exam unremarkable
data_table.FBC yesterday: WCC 2.8 x10^9/L (baseline 4.5), ANC 1.4 x10^9/L (baseline 2.2), lymphocytes 1.2 x10^9/L, Hb 148 g/L, platelets 240 x10^9/L, CRP <5 mg/L
data_table.Prior monitoring: ANC 2.0-2.4 x10^9/L on prior 2 monthly counts

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in clozapine management?

options.text: Give subcutaneous filgrastim 300 microgram daily for five days empirically and continue clozapine at current dose with monthly full blood count reviews and outpatient follow-up
options.rationale: Filgrastim is used in confirmed severe neutropenia (ANC below 0.5) or persistent moderate neutropenia; not indicated in amber range with a well patient. (Source: TGA Clozapine Monitoring Guideline)

options.text: Stop clozapine immediately and admit for daily full blood count for at least 14 days with reverse barrier nursing and empirical broad spectrum antibiotics started before culture results
options.rationale: Immediate cessation and admission is for ANC below 0.5 x10^9/L (severe neutropenia); ANC 1.4 is amber not red. (Source: TGA Clozapine Monitoring Guideline)

options.text: Reduce clozapine to 300 mg nocte and repeat full blood count monthly with clinical review, allow patient home with instructions to attend if febrile at any point subsequent
options.rationale: Dose reduction alone is not standard; weekly FBC is required in amber range and dose is unchanged unless further drop. (Source: TGA Clozapine Monitoring Guideline)

options.text: Continue clozapine at current dose, repeat full blood count in one week and check for infective source with C-reactive protein and mid-stream urine at the same interval
options.rationale: ANC 1.0-1.5 x10^9/L is the amber (Watching) range: continue clozapine, repeat FBC weekly, monitor for infection. (Source: TGA Clozapine Monitoring Guideline)

options.text: Stop clozapine and switch to oral olanzapine 20 mg nocte the same day, restart clozapine only after two weeks of ANC above 2.0 x10^9/L with weekly review of the transition
options.rationale: Switching antipsychotic in a stable patient with amber-range neutropenia is not indicated and risks psychotic relapse. (Source: TGA Clozapine Monitoring Guideline)

explanation.summary: Clozapine can cause neutropenia and agranulocytosis (1 to 2 percent lifetime risk of agranulocytosis) requiring mandatory haematological monitoring. Australian monitoring (Clopine/Clozaril/Zaponex Patient Monitoring): weekly FBC for the first 18 weeks, then fortnightly to 52 weeks, then 4 weekly indefinitely. Traffic light system in Australia: Green (WCC >=3.5 and ANC >=2.0 x10^9/L) continue at current schedule; Amber (WCC 3.0-3.5 or ANC 1.5-2.0) continue with twice weekly FBC; Red (WCC below 3.0 or ANC below 1.5) stop clozapine and daily FBC (formal cut-offs vary by monitoring service - Clopine Red is WCC below 3.0 x10^9/L or ANC below 1.5 x10^9/L). ANC below 0.5 is severe agranulocytosis requiring reverse isolation and haematology involvement. Benign ethnic neutropenia (common in African, Middle Eastern, some Mediterranean descent) has separate lower thresholds under specialist supervision.
key_points: Clopine Red = WCC <3.0 or ANC <1.5 x10^9/L: stop clozapine, daily FBC.
ANC 1.0-1.5 = investigate for infection, weekly FBC.
ANC below 0.5 = severe agranulocytosis: haematology, reverse isolation.
explanation.pearls: Clozapine monitoring - ANC 1.4 x10^9/L in a well patient with no infection is in the amber range at RANZCP: continue clozapine, repeat FBC weekly and screen for occult infection - do not stop the drug.

subtopic_detail: Choice of benzodiazepine for alcohol withdrawal in the setting of established cirrhotic liver disease
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 58 year old man from the emergency department at 23:00 with alcohol withdrawal. He has drunk 15 standard drinks of spirits daily for the last 20 years and stopped 36 hours ago because he ran out. He has a diagnosis of alcoholic cirrhosis on outpatient follow-up with a MELD of 14. He takes no regular medications.

On assessment he has pulse rate 118 per minute, blood pressure 168/98 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 per minute, oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air, temperature 37.4 degC. He is agitated and diaphoretic with visual hallucinations of small animals in the corner. Alcohol Withdrawal Scale score is 14. He has coarse tremor of the outstretched hands, no seizures. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations are unremarkable. Abdomen shows mild non-tender ascites and no encephalopathy features today. Investigations: haemoglobin 118 g/L, platelet count 82 x10^9/L, INR 1.4, albumin 28 g/L, bilirubin 40 micromol/L, aspartate aminotransferase 92 U/L, ammonia 68 micromol/L (below 55). Blood glucose 5.2 mmol/L. Full blood count and urea and electrolytes otherwise unremarkable. Thiamine 300 mg IV has been given in the emergency department.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118 /min, blood pressure 168/98 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 /min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 37.4 degC
data_table.Mental state: Agitated, diaphoretic, visual hallucinations of small animals, AWS 14, coarse tremor, no seizures
data_table.Bloods: Hb 118 g/L, platelets 82 x10^9/L, INR 1.4, albumin 28 g/L, bilirubin 40 micromol/L, AST 92 U/L, ammonia 68 micromol/L (<55), glucose 5.2 mmol/L
data_table.History: 15 standard drinks/day 20 years, stopped 36 h ago, alcoholic cirrhosis MELD 14

lead_in: Which benzodiazepine regimen is most appropriate?

options.text: Intramuscular midazolam 5 mg two hourly titrated to Alcohol Withdrawal Scale under 5 with continued thiamine 300 mg intravenous daily for three days as ongoing Wernicke prophylaxis
options.rationale: Midazolam is short-acting and unsuitable for withdrawal maintenance; intramuscular route has erratic absorption. (Source: Australian Alcohol Guidelines (NHMRC))

options.text: Oral diazepam 20 mg every two hours titrated to Alcohol Withdrawal Scale under 5 with continued thiamine 300 mg intravenous daily for three days as ongoing Wernicke prophylaxis
options.rationale: Diazepam has active metabolites (nordiazepam) that accumulate in cirrhosis, risking prolonged sedation and precipitating hepatic encephalopathy. (Source: Australian Alcohol Guidelines (NHMRC))

options.text: Oral oxazepam 30 mg every four hours titrated to Alcohol Withdrawal Scale under 5 with continued thiamine 300 mg intravenous daily for three days as ongoing Wernicke prophylaxis
options.rationale: Oxazepam has no active metabolites and non-hepatic metabolism (glucuronidation), making it safer than diazepam in cirrhosis. (Source: Australian Alcohol Guidelines (NHMRC))

options.text: Oral chlordiazepoxide 25 mg every four hours titrated to Alcohol Withdrawal Scale under 5 with continued thiamine 300 mg intravenous daily for three days as ongoing Wernicke prophylaxis
options.rationale: Chlordiazepoxide has active metabolites and hepatic metabolism, so it accumulates in cirrhosis; not preferred here. (Source: Australian Alcohol Guidelines (NHMRC))

options.text: Intravenous phenobarbitone 130 mg two hourly titrated to Alcohol Withdrawal Scale under 5 with continued thiamine 300 mg intravenous daily for three days as ongoing Wernicke prophylaxis
options.rationale: Phenobarbitone is reserved for benzodiazepine-refractory delirium tremens; it is not first line and requires close monitoring. (Source: Australian Alcohol Guidelines (NHMRC))

explanation.summary: Alcohol withdrawal severity is graded on the Alcohol Withdrawal Scale or CIWA-Ar. Mild withdrawal (score below 8): symptomatic care, no benzodiazepine needed. Moderate to severe (score 8 or above): benzodiazepine loading and symptom-triggered dosing. Diazepam 10 to 20 mg orally 2 hourly is first line in patients with normal liver function due to long half-life and active metabolites providing smooth wean. In cirrhosis, hepatic encephalopathy risk and metabolite accumulation make short-acting agents metabolised by glucuronidation (LOT: lorazepam, oxazepam, temazepam) preferred; oxazepam 15 to 30 mg orally 4 hourly is the Australian standard in cirrhosis. Thiamine 300 mg IV daily for 3-5 days before any glucose to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy. Delirium tremens (autonomic instability, hyperthermia, hallucinations) has mortality of 5-15 percent untreated; treat aggressively with high-dose benzodiazepines, IV fluid and monitoring. Phenobarbitone is second line for benzodiazepine-refractory delirium tremens.
key_points: Diazepam is first line for alcohol withdrawal in normal liver function.
In cirrhosis, use LOT (lorazepam, oxazepam, temazepam) - glucuronidation not oxidative metabolism.
Thiamine 300 mg IV daily 3-5 days before glucose to prevent Wernicke.
explanation.pearls: Alcohol withdrawal in cirrhosis at NHMRC uses oxazepam 15-30 mg orally 4 hourly (glucuronidated, no active metabolites) instead of diazepam - active nordiazepam metabolite of diazepam accumulates and can precipitate hepatic encephalopathy.

subtopic_detail: First-line antidepressant selection and monitoring in a depressed adolescent with suicidal ideation but no intent
stem:
You are the child and adolescent psychiatry registrar reviewing a 15 year old girl in the community adolescent mental health service with an eight week history of low mood, anhedonia, poor sleep, poor appetite with 3 kg weight loss and worsening school attendance. She has passive thoughts of "not wanting to wake up" occurring several days per week over the last two weeks. She has no plan and no active suicidal intent, no self-harm history, and she attends the appointment with her mother.

She has no medical history and no substance use. Her mother reports no family history of bipolar affective disorder. There is no first-degree family history of suicide. She has been attending cognitive behavioural therapy weekly for six weeks without improvement in symptoms. Kessler-10 today is 34. Mental state examination reveals a tearful adolescent with reduced eye contact, reduced psychomotor activity, congruent affect, thoughts of hopelessness, and passive suicidal ideation with no plan and no intent. Cognition is preserved and there is no psychotic phenomenology. Physical examination and thyroid function tests are normal. Full blood count, urea and electrolytes, iron studies within normal limits. She has never taken psychotropic medication.

data_table.Mental state: Tearful, reduced eye contact, reduced psychomotor activity, congruent affect, hopelessness, passive SI without plan or intent, no psychosis
data_table.Symptoms: 8 weeks low mood, anhedonia, poor sleep, poor appetite (3 kg weight loss), poor school attendance
data_table.Suicide risk: Passive SI days per week for 2 weeks, no plan, no intent, no self-harm history, no first-degree suicide history
data_table.Prior treatment: Weekly CBT for 6 weeks, no improvement
data_table.Baseline investigations: TFTs, FBC, UEC, iron studies within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her treatment plan?

options.text: Commence oral sertraline 25 mg mane increasing to 50 mg after one week with weekly clinical review for four weeks and safety planning documented in collaboration with her mother
options.rationale: Sertraline is used in adolescent MDD but has weaker adolescent evidence than fluoxetine; fluoxetine is first line in adolescents at RANZCP. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Depression)

options.text: Commence oral fluoxetine 10 mg mane increasing to 20 mg after one week with weekly clinical review for four weeks and safety planning documented in collaboration with her mother
options.rationale: Fluoxetine is the only SSRI with TGA and RANZCP recommendation for adolescent MDD after CBT failure; requires weekly review for suicidality first month. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Depression)

options.text: Commence oral venlafaxine extended release 37.5 mg mane increasing to 75 mg after one week with weekly clinical review for four weeks and safety planning documented in collaboration with her mother
options.rationale: Venlafaxine has an FDA black box warning in adolescents with increased suicidality; not first line for adolescent MDD. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Depression)

options.text: Continue psychological therapy only, arrange interpersonal therapy weekly for eight weeks and defer any pharmacotherapy until improvement or worsening at review before adding medication
options.rationale: CBT for 6 weeks without improvement in moderate to severe adolescent MDD is trial failure; RANZCP recommends adding fluoxetine, not continuing psychotherapy alone. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Depression)

options.text: Admit to adolescent inpatient psychiatric ward for observation and safety and defer commencement of pharmacotherapy until multidisciplinary team review on the ward next week
options.rationale: Passive SI without plan or intent, with family support and no self-harm history, does not require inpatient admission; outpatient management with fluoxetine and safety planning is appropriate. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Depression)

explanation.summary: Adolescent major depression (age 12-17) is managed with a stepped approach. Mild MDD: psychoeducation, sleep hygiene, exercise, brief psychological intervention. Moderate to severe MDD or mild MDD failing brief intervention: cognitive behavioural therapy or interpersonal therapy for adolescents as first line for 6 to 8 weeks. If inadequate response or severe presentation, add pharmacotherapy. Fluoxetine 10 to 20 mg daily is the only SSRI with TGA and RANZCP endorsement as first-line pharmacotherapy in adolescents (based on TADS trial data). Sertraline is second line. Venlafaxine and paroxetine are avoided in adolescents due to increased suicidality risk. Weekly clinical review for the first four weeks of any antidepressant in adolescents is mandatory (increased short-term risk of suicidality in the first month). Safety planning should be documented and shared with parents/carers. Combination of CBT and fluoxetine is more effective than either alone (TADS trial).
key_points: Fluoxetine 10-20 mg is first-line adolescent SSRI (TADS trial, TGA and RANZCP endorsed).
Weekly review for 4 weeks after starting antidepressant in adolescents.
Avoid venlafaxine and paroxetine in adolescents (suicidality risk).
explanation.pearls: Adolescent MDD failing CBT: add fluoxetine 10 mg daily and review weekly for 4 weeks - fluoxetine is the only SSRI RANZCP endorses first line in adolescents, not sertraline.

subtopic_detail: Antipsychotic choice in a first-episode psychosis in a young man with metabolic and adherence considerations
stem:
You are the early intervention psychiatry registrar reviewing a 21 year old man referred by his general practitioner with a six week history of paranoid delusions that his housemates are poisoning his food, third-person auditory hallucinations, and social withdrawal. He has smoked five to ten cones of cannabis daily for the last three years but has not used other substances. He is otherwise well. He lives with his parents who are supportive and will assist with medication supervision.

His body mass index is 22 kg per square metre and blood pressure 122/76 mmHg. Family history includes obesity, type 2 diabetes in his father and hypertension in his mother; no psychiatric family history. Mental state examination reveals a well groomed young man with reduced eye contact, restricted affect, third person auditory hallucinations, paranoid delusional content and no thoughts of harm to self or others. Insight is limited. Cognitive screening is unimpaired. Investigations: fasting glucose 4.8 mmol/L, HbA1c 5.4 percent, lipid profile within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone 2.8 mIU/L, prolactin within normal limits, electrocardiogram QTc 420 milliseconds, urine drug screen positive for cannabinoids only. He is very concerned about weight gain from psychiatric medication and has said he will not take a medication that causes weight gain.

data_table.Mental state: Well groomed, reduced eye contact, restricted affect, 3rd person AH, paranoid delusions (poisoning), no HI/SI, limited insight, cognition intact
data_table.Substance use: Cannabis 5-10 cones daily for 3 years, no other substances, urine cannabinoids positive only
data_table.Family history: Obesity, T2DM (father), HTN (mother), no psychiatric FHx
data_table.Baseline metabolics: Fasting glucose 4.8 mmol/L, HbA1c 5.4%, lipids normal, TSH 2.8, prolactin normal, ECG QTc 420 ms
data_table.Preferences: Very concerned about weight gain, will not take medication that causes weight gain, parents supervise medications

lead_in: Which oral antipsychotic is most appropriate to commence?

options.text: Olanzapine 5 mg nocte titrating to 10 mg after one week and refer to youth alcohol and other drugs service for cannabis brief intervention alongside early intervention psychiatry follow-up
options.rationale: Olanzapine has the highest weight gain and dyslipidaemia burden of second-generation antipsychotics and directly conflicts with this patient's stated preference and adherence risk. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Schizophrenia)

options.text: Aripiprazole 10 mg mane titrating to 15 mg after one week and refer to youth alcohol and other drugs service for cannabis brief intervention alongside early intervention psychiatry follow-up
options.rationale: Aripiprazole has the lowest weight-gain profile among second-generation antipsychotics and is preferred first-line for FEP where metabolic risk and adherence concern medication acceptance. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Schizophrenia)

options.text: Haloperidol 2 mg twice daily titrating to 5 mg twice daily after one week and refer to youth alcohol and other drugs service for cannabis brief intervention alongside early intervention follow-up
options.rationale: First-generation antipsychotics are not preferred first line in FEP due to higher extrapyramidal side-effect burden; second-generation agents are preferred. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Schizophrenia)

options.text: Risperidone 1 mg twice daily titrating to 3 mg twice daily after one week and refer to youth alcohol and other drugs service for cannabis brief intervention alongside early intervention follow-up
options.rationale: Risperidone has a dose-related risk of extrapyramidal side effects and prolactin elevation with reduced acceptability in a young man. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Schizophrenia)

options.text: Clozapine 12.5 mg mane titrating over 2 weeks and refer to youth alcohol and other drugs service for cannabis brief intervention alongside early intervention psychiatry follow-up
options.rationale: Clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia (failure of two adequate trials of other antipsychotics); not first line for FEP. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Schizophrenia)

explanation.summary: First-episode psychosis is a critical intervention window where antipsychotic choice balances efficacy, tolerability, metabolic risk and patient preference to maximise adherence. RANZCP recommends second-generation antipsychotics as first line, matched to patient factors. Aripiprazole has the lowest weight-gain profile (partial dopamine agonist), no prolactin elevation and minimal QTc effect, making it preferred for young men with metabolic risk factors or concern about weight gain. Olanzapine and clozapine carry the highest metabolic burden. Risperidone has dose-related extrapyramidal and prolactin effects. Cannabis use is common in FEP and worsens the psychotic prodrome; concurrent referral to youth AOD services for brief intervention is standard. Depot antipsychotics can be considered early to support adherence. Metabolic monitoring at baseline, 6 weeks, 3 months, then annually is mandated (weight, BP, fasting glucose, lipids).
key_points: Second-generation antipsychotic first line in FEP, matched to patient factors.
Aripiprazole has the lowest weight-gain and prolactin profile; olanzapine the highest.
Refer to youth AOD service concurrently for cannabis brief intervention.
explanation.pearls: FEP in a young man with cannabis use and stated aversion to weight-gaining medications: aripiprazole 10 mg is preferred over olanzapine because aripiprazole has the lowest metabolic burden and best supports adherence.

subtopic_detail: Emergency department risk assessment and disposition for repeated self-harm in emotionally unstable personality disorder
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar assessing a 26 year old woman brought in by ambulance after superficial cutting of the left forearm with a razor blade after an argument with her partner. She has a diagnosis of emotionally unstable personality disorder and depression. She has presented to the department five times in the last three months, always with superficial cutting after interpersonal stressors, and has always been discharged home after brief assessment.

She is under the care of a community mental health team with a case manager and attends weekly dialectical behaviour therapy. On arrival she has pulse rate 82 per minute, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 per minute, oxygen saturation 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degC. Wound is superficial with clean edges, does not require suturing, and dressings are applied. She is engaged in conversation, tearful, remorseful about the cutting and denies suicidal ideation now. Her case manager has been contacted and agrees she is at her usual baseline. Her mother and partner are in the waiting room and will provide support at home overnight. No alcohol or other substance use in the last week. Her most recent DBT session was two days ago. She has a written safety plan in her handbag which she brought with her tonight.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 82 /min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Wound: Superficial forearm cutting, clean edges, no suturing required, dressings applied
data_table.Mental state: Engaged, tearful, remorseful, denies SI now, no acute intoxication, at baseline per case manager
data_table.History: 5 presentations in 3 months, always superficial cutting after interpersonal stressors, always discharged after brief assessment
data_table.Community supports: Case manager, weekly DBT (last session 2 days ago), mother and partner supportive, written safety plan on person

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Wound care and discharge home to mother and partner overnight with liaison to community case manager for next-day contact and safety planning review, and update her existing crisis plan
options.rationale: Repeated superficial self-harm in EUPD without acute high-risk features is best managed in community per RANZCP; ED admission does not improve outcomes and can reinforce escalation. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline BPD)

options.text: Admission under the Mental Health Act to the acute inpatient psychiatric unit for a minimum of 72 hours observation and reassessment before discharge back to community care
options.rationale: Involuntary admission is not indicated: she is at baseline, has supports and denies suicidality; inpatient admission worsens outcomes in EUPD. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline BPD)

options.text: Admission to short-stay unit for 24 hours observation and initiation of oral quetiapine 100 mg nocte as a mood stabilising augmentation before discharge back to community follow-up
options.rationale: Pharmacotherapy is not first line for EUPD and quetiapine sedation increases self-harm reinforcement; RANZCP recommends against routine pharmacotherapy. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline BPD)

options.text: Admit voluntarily to the psychiatric intensive care unit for 48 hours to break the cycle of frequent presentations and provide a period of intensive observation and treatment planning
options.rationale: Intensive care admission is disproportionate and reinforces presentation escalation; DBT plus community support is the evidence-based pathway. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline BPD)

options.text: Discharge home with instruction to attend the general practitioner next week for review of her ongoing risk without contacting the case manager tonight or updating the current safety plan
options.rationale: Discharge without case manager liaison or safety plan review misses the opportunity to reinforce structured support and update the crisis plan. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline BPD)

explanation.summary: Emotionally unstable personality disorder (EUPD, ICD-11) or borderline personality disorder is characterised by pervasive instability of affect, interpersonal relationships and self-image, with impulsivity and recurrent self-harm. Repeated brief emergency department presentations after interpersonal stressors are typical. RANZCP evidence-based guideline: psychotherapy (dialectical behaviour therapy, mentalisation based therapy) is first-line treatment. Pharmacotherapy is not routine and should be time-limited if used for a comorbid disorder. Hospital admission does not improve outcomes and can reinforce the pattern of self-harm as help-seeking; brief admission (24 to 72 hours) is reserved for objectively high risk of suicide (specific plan, means, escalation from usual pattern) or acute psychosocial crisis without other supports. In the ED, wound care, brief supportive assessment, validation of distress, safety plan review, and rapid linkage back to the community team is the recommended pathway. Family and case manager should be engaged.
key_points: DBT and MBT are first-line psychotherapies in EUPD; pharmacotherapy not routine.
Admission does not improve outcomes and can reinforce escalation of self-harm.
ED role: wound care, validation, safety plan review, community team linkage.
explanation.pearls: Recurrent superficial self-harm in EUPD at baseline: wound care, safety plan review, discharge to family with case manager next-day contact - admission reinforces the pattern and does not improve outcomes per RANZCP.

sources.label: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder

subtopic_detail: Recognition and management of refeeding hypophosphataemia during nutritional rehabilitation of severe anorexia nervosa
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 19 year old woman admitted 48 hours ago from an eating disorders outpatient clinic with anorexia nervosa restricting subtype for nutritional rehabilitation. Body mass index on admission was 12.8 kg per square metre with a two year history of restriction and 30 percent weight loss over six months. She has been medically stable except for orthostatic bradycardia on admission.

She has been started on a graded refeeding protocol with continuous enteral feed via nasogastric tube commencing at 20 kcal per kilogram per day (1000 kcal per day today) as per the local unit protocol, with thiamine 300 mg intravenous daily and a multivitamin. On assessment this morning she has pulse rate 62 per minute, blood pressure 96/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.4 degC. She is alert but reports increased fatigue and mild lower limb weakness climbing to her bed. This morning's bloods (48 hours after commencement of feeds): serum phosphate 0.42 mmol/L (0.75 to 1.5), magnesium 0.62 mmol/L (0.7 to 1.0), potassium 3.2 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.0), calcium 2.28 mmol/L (2.10 to 2.60), glucose 4.4 mmol/L, urea 3.2 mmol/L, creatinine 62 micromol/L. Electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm with prolonged PR interval 220 milliseconds and normal QTc.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 62 /min, blood pressure 96/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.4 degC
data_table.Symptoms: Increased fatigue, mild lower limb weakness climbing to bed
data_table.Refeeding regimen: NG continuous feed 20 kcal/kg/day (1000 kcal/day), thiamine 300 mg IV daily, multivitamin
data_table.Bloods (48 h): Phosphate 0.42 mmol/L (0.75-1.5), Mg 0.62 mmol/L (0.7-1.0), K 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), Ca 2.28 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), glucose 4.4 mmol/L, urea 3.2 mmol/L, creatinine 62 micromol/L
data_table.ECG: Sinus rhythm, PR 220 ms, normal QTc
data_table.Background: AN restricting subtype, BMI 12.8, 30% weight loss in 6 months, orthostatic bradycardia on admission

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Cease all enteral feed for 24 hours and give intravenous 5 percent dextrose 100 mL per hour with intravenous phosphate 30 mmol in 500 mL over 12 hours and repeat electrolytes in 8 hours
options.rationale: Complete feed cessation loses accumulated nutritional gains; graded reduction with correction is preferred; dextrose stimulates insulin and worsens intracellular shift. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Eating Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Eating Disorders

options.text: Continue enteral feed at current rate of 20 kcal per kilogram per day and give oral phosphate 500 mg three times daily as monotherapy with repeat bloods in 24 hours before further adjustment
options.rationale: Continued full feed with symptomatic hypophosphataemia risks progression to cardiac and neurological failure; slow feed reduction and IV correction is needed. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Eating Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Eating Disorders

options.text: Increase enteral feed to 40 kcal per kilogram per day to accelerate nutritional recovery and give oral phosphate 500 mg twice daily with repeat bloods in 24 hours before further adjustment
options.rationale: Increasing feed will worsen refeeding syndrome; the pathophysiology is intracellular phosphate shift driven by insulin surge with feeding. (Source: RANZCOG Clinical Practice Guidelines Eating Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Eating Disorders

options.text: Reduce enteral feed to 10 kcal per kilogram per day and give intravenous phosphate 30 mmol in 500 mL normal saline over 6 hours plus magnesium sulfate 20 mmol and potassium chloride 20 mmol
options.rationale: Symptomatic refeeding syndrome with phosphate 0.42 mmol/L requires calorie reduction plus IV phosphate, magnesium and potassium replacement per RANZCP eating disorders guideline. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Eating Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Eating Disorders

options.text: Continue feed at current rate and defer any electrolyte correction until phosphate falls below 0.3 mmol per L or symptoms of respiratory or cardiac failure develop clinically at bedside
options.rationale: Waiting for phosphate below 0.3 mmol/L or organ failure risks catastrophic outcome; refeeding syndrome is progressive and needs early correction. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Eating Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Eating Disorders

explanation.summary: Refeeding syndrome is the metabolic response to reintroduction of nutrition in a malnourished patient, driven by insulin release causing intracellular shift of phosphate, magnesium and potassium and thiamine consumption. Risk factors: BMI below 16, 15 percent weight loss over 3 months, minimal nutrition intake over 10 days, low pre-refeed electrolytes. Diagnosis is a fall of at least 30 percent in serum phosphate from baseline or an absolute phosphate below 0.6 mmol/L. Australian practice starts refeeding at 20 kcal/kg/day in high-risk anorexia nervosa (previously as low as 10 kcal/kg/day, but current evidence supports 20 kcal/kg/day with intensive electrolyte monitoring and correction). Prevention and management: thiamine 300 mg IV daily for 5 days before or with feed commencement, daily electrolytes for the first week, prompt replacement of phosphate, magnesium and potassium. When refeeding syndrome develops: reduce feed rate to 10 kcal/kg/day, correct electrolytes intravenously if symptomatic or severe, then re-titrate feed upward as electrolytes normalise. Ongoing multidisciplinary eating disorders team involvement is essential.
key_points: Refeeding syndrome: intracellular shift of phosphate, magnesium, potassium with feeding.
Severe hypophosphataemia (below 0.6 mmol/L) or symptomatic: IV replacement, reduce feed.
Thiamine 300 mg IV daily 5 days precedes or accompanies refeeding.
explanation.pearls: Refeeding hypophosphataemia at 48 hours with phosphate 0.42 mmol/L in anorexia nervosa: reduce feed to 10 kcal/kg/day and give IV phosphate 30 mmol plus magnesium and potassium - do not increase or continue full feed rate.

subtopic_detail: Initial fluid resuscitation and insulin timing in adult new-onset diabetic ketoacidosis
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar reviewing a 22 year old woman brought in by her partner with 12 hours of nausea, vomiting, thirst and confusion. She was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes at age 12 and takes basal insulin degludec 24 units nocte with prandial insulin aspart. She stopped her insulin four days ago because of a stomach flu and inability to eat.

On assessment she has pulse rate 132 per minute, blood pressure 96/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 per minute, oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degC. She has dry mucous membranes, deep sighing respirations, capillary refill 3 seconds and Glasgow Coma Scale 14 (E4 V4 M6). Point of care blood glucose is 26 mmol/L, capillary ketones 4.8 mmol/L. Venous blood gas: pH 7.12, bicarbonate 10 mmol/L, potassium 5.6 mmol/L, sodium 132 mmol/L, chloride 98 mmol/L, lactate 2.6 mmol/L. Urea 12 mmol/L, creatinine 108 micromol/L (baseline 62). Electrocardiogram shows sinus tachycardia with peaked T waves in lead V4 and V5.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 132 /min, blood pressure 96/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Neurology: GCS 14 (E4 V4 M6), alert but confused
data_table.Perfusion: Dry mucous membranes, capillary refill 3 sec, cool peripheries
data_table.Point of care: Blood glucose 26 mmol/L, capillary ketones 4.8 mmol/L
data_table.Venous blood gas: pH 7.12, bicarbonate 10 mmol/L, K 5.6 mmol/L, Na 132 mmol/L, Cl 98 mmol/L, lactate 2.6 mmol/L
data_table.ECG: Sinus tachycardia, peaked T waves V4-V5
data_table.History: T1DM 10 years, degludec 24 units nocte + aspart, stopped insulin 4 days ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin lispro 10 units immediately plus intravenous 0.9 percent sodium chloride 1 L over 4 hours and repeat capillary ketones and glucose after 2 hours of therapy
options.rationale: Subcutaneous insulin is only used for uncomplicated mild DKA (pH above 7.25); severe DKA requires IV insulin infusion for controlled titration. (Source: Australian Diabetes Society DKA Guideline)

options.text: Intravenous 0.9 percent sodium chloride 1 L over 30 minutes with intravenous insulin infusion 0.1 unit per kilogram per hour commenced simultaneously with the first litre of fluid resuscitation
options.rationale: Insulin is delayed until the first litre of fluid has been given to allow expansion of extracellular volume and to avoid precipitating dangerous hypokalaemia. (Source: Australian Diabetes Society DKA Guideline)

options.text: Intravenous 0.45 percent sodium chloride 500 mL per hour with intravenous insulin infusion 0.05 unit per kilogram per hour and potassium chloride 40 mmol per L in the fluid bag started immediately
options.rationale: Half normal saline is not first-line initial resuscitation fluid; normal saline is preferred first hour; insulin dose is 0.1 U/kg/h. (Source: Australian Diabetes Society DKA Guideline)

options.text: Intravenous 0.9 percent sodium chloride 1 L over 30 minutes with intravenous sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol bolus over 30 minutes given the venous pH of 7.12 to reverse the metabolic acidosis
options.rationale: Bicarbonate is only considered for pH below 6.9 in DKA due to risk of paradoxical CSF acidosis and cerebral oedema. (Source: Australian Diabetes Society DKA Guideline)

options.text: Intravenous 0.9 percent sodium chloride 1 L over 30 minutes then reassess, commence fixed-rate intravenous insulin infusion 0.1 unit per kilogram per hour after the first litre of fluid
options.rationale: ADS/JBDS-IP DKA protocol: crystalloid resuscitation first litre over 30 min, then IV insulin at 0.1 U/kg/h; potassium replacement withheld until K below 5.5 mmol/L. (Source: Australian Diabetes Society DKA Guideline)

explanation.summary: Diabetic ketoacidosis diagnosis: glucose above 11 mmol/L (or known diabetes), venous pH below 7.3 or bicarbonate below 15, and ketones above 3 mmol/L or urine ketones 2+. Severity: severe if pH below 7.0 or bicarbonate below 5 or GCS below 12. Management (Australian Diabetes Society / JBDS-IP): first litre of 0.9 percent saline over 30 to 60 minutes, then second litre with potassium chloride 40 mmol added (if serum K 3.5 to 5.5 mmol/L). Fixed-rate insulin infusion 0.1 U/kg/h commenced after the first litre. Add 10 percent dextrose 125 mL/h when glucose falls below 14 mmol/L (continuing insulin infusion to clear ketones). Monitor capillary ketones, glucose, potassium and blood gas hourly. Ketone clearance rate should be 0.5 mmol/L/h; if not, increase insulin. Bicarbonate is reserved for pH below 6.9 in extreme circumstances. Precipitants (infection, missed insulin, MI, pancreatitis) must be sought and treated.
key_points: DKA fluid: 0.9 percent saline first litre over 30-60 min, then with K 40 mmol added.
Fixed-rate IV insulin 0.1 U/kg/h after first litre of fluid.
Bicarbonate only for pH below 6.9; SC insulin only for mild DKA (pH above 7.25).
explanation.pearls: Adult DKA: give 1 L normal saline over 30 min first, then start IV insulin at 0.1 U/kg/h - insulin follows the first litre of fluid to avoid precipitating hypokalaemia.

subtopic_detail: Antiplatelet strategy and invasive timing decision in a high-risk non-ST elevation myocardial infarction
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 62 year old man in the coronary care unit who presented three hours ago with two hours of central crushing chest pain radiating to the left arm at rest. He is now pain free after morphine and sublingual glyceryl trinitrate. He has type 2 diabetes, hypertension and hyperlipidaemia. Regular medications are metformin, perindopril, atorvastatin and aspirin 100 mg daily.

On assessment he has pulse rate 88 per minute, blood pressure 138/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degC. Cardiovascular examination reveals normal heart sounds with no added sounds, clear chest and no peripheral oedema. Electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm with 1 mm ST depression and T wave inversion in leads V4 to V6 (unchanged from the ED tracing). High sensitivity troponin at presentation 240 ng/L (below 14) with three-hour repeat 610 ng/L. GRACE risk score is 148. Full blood count, electrolytes and estimated glomerular filtration rate 78 mL per minute are within normal limits. Bedside echocardiography shows preserved left ventricular function with mild anteroseptal hypokinesis. He is on aspirin 300 mg loading dose from ED and heparin 5000 units subcutaneous.

data_table.Chest pain: Central crushing 2 h radiating to left arm at rest, now pain free after morphine + GTN
data_table.ECG: Sinus rhythm, 1 mm ST depression and T inversion V4-V6 (unchanged from ED)
data_table.Echo: Preserved LV function, mild anteroseptal hypokinesis
data_table.Bloods: FBC, UEC within normal limits, eGFR 78 mL/min
data_table.Given so far: Aspirin 300 mg PO in ED, heparin 5000 units SC
data_table.Background: T2DM, HTN, dyslipidaemia; on metformin, perindopril, atorvastatin, aspirin 100 mg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Clopidogrel 300 mg loading dose orally with therapeutic enoxaparin 1 mg per kilogram twice daily and coronary angiography within 72 hours for planned percutaneous coronary intervention
options.rationale: Ticagrelor is preferred over clopidogrel in NSTEMI unless contraindicated; angiography within 24 hours for GRACE >140. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ ACS Guidelines 2016 (update 2022))

options.text: Ticagrelor 180 mg loading dose orally with therapeutic enoxaparin 1 mg per kilogram twice daily and coronary angiography within 24 hours for planned percutaneous coronary intervention
options.rationale: GRACE >140 is high risk NSTEMI: DAPT plus therapeutic anticoagulation with invasive angiography within 24 hours per NHFA. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ ACS Guidelines 2016 (update 2022))

options.text: Prasugrel 60 mg loading dose orally with therapeutic enoxaparin 1 mg per kilogram twice daily and coronary angiography within 24 hours for planned percutaneous coronary intervention
options.rationale: Prasugrel is reserved for PCI-treated patients where coronary anatomy is known; not preferred before angiography (increased bleeding without anatomical guidance). (Source: NHFA/CSANZ ACS Guidelines 2016 (update 2022))

options.text: Ticagrelor 180 mg loading dose orally with therapeutic enoxaparin 1 mg per kilogram twice daily and coronary angiography within 72 hours for planned percutaneous coronary intervention
options.rationale: 72 hour angiography is intermediate risk (GRACE 109-140); GRACE 148 is high risk (>140) mandating angiography within 24 hours. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ ACS Guidelines 2016 (update 2022))

options.text: Continue current aspirin monotherapy and enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily prophylaxis and arrange outpatient exercise stress test in one week for further risk stratification
options.rationale: Ischaemia testing is not appropriate after confirmed NSTEMI (rising troponin, dynamic ECG); invasive angiography is indicated. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ ACS Guidelines 2016 (update 2022))

explanation.summary: NSTEMI diagnosis: rise or fall in troponin above 99th centile plus one of: symptoms of ischaemia, new ischaemic ECG changes, imaging evidence of new loss of viable myocardium, or intracoronary thrombus at angiography. Risk stratification uses GRACE score: low risk (below 109) conservative or delayed invasive above 72 hours; intermediate risk (109 to 140) angiography within 72 hours; high risk (above 140) angiography within 24 hours. Very high risk (haemodynamic instability, cardiogenic shock, recurrent angina, life-threatening arrhythmia, mechanical complications) mandates urgent angiography within 2 hours. Dual antiplatelet therapy: aspirin (300 mg load then 100 mg daily) plus a P2Y12 inhibitor. Ticagrelor (180 mg load then 90 mg twice daily) is preferred over clopidogrel in NSTEMI due to superior efficacy in PLATO trial. Prasugrel is used after diagnostic angiography when PCI is planned. Anticoagulation with enoxaparin, unfractionated heparin, bivalirudin or fondaparinux is standard. Beta blocker, ACE inhibitor and high-intensity statin post-MI as standard therapies.
key_points: GRACE above 140 = high risk NSTEMI: angiography within 24 hours.
Ticagrelor preferred over clopidogrel in NSTEMI (PLATO trial).
Prasugrel reserved for PCI-treated patients with known anatomy.
explanation.pearls: NSTEMI with GRACE 148 gets ticagrelor 180 mg load, therapeutic enoxaparin and coronary angiography within 24 hours - GRACE above 140 is high risk requiring early invasive strategy per NHFA.

subtopic_detail: Antibiotic selection for severe community-acquired pneumonia in a nursing home resident
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 78 year old woman transferred from her residential aged care facility with two days of fever, productive cough and worsening confusion. She has hypertension, atrial fibrillation on apixaban, mild cognitive impairment and no known drug allergies. She was ambulant with a walker until today.

On assessment she has pulse rate 118 per minute, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 per minute, oxygen saturation 89 percent on room air, temperature 38.9 degC. She is drowsy but rousable and disoriented in time and place. Chest examination reveals bronchial breath sounds and crackles in the right mid zone. Investigations: haemoglobin 118 g/L, white cell count 18.2 x10^9/L, platelet count 240 x10^9/L, C-reactive protein 340 mg/L, urea 12 mmol/L, creatinine 118 micromol/L (baseline 82), sodium 132 mmol/L, potassium 4.4 mmol/L, lactate 3.2 mmol/L. Arterial blood gas on 4 L per minute nasal prongs: pH 7.32, PaCO2 32 mmHg, PaO2 62 mmHg, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L. Chest X-ray shows right middle lobe consolidation. Urine legionella antigen pending. CURB-65 is 5 (confusion, urea >7, RR >=30, SBP <90, age >=65).

data_table.Mental state: Drowsy but rousable, disoriented in time and place
data_table.Chest: Bronchial breath sounds and crackles right mid zone
data_table.Bloods: Hb 118 g/L, WCC 18.2 x10^9/L, platelets 240 x10^9/L, CRP 340 mg/L, urea 12 mmol/L, creatinine 118 micromol/L (baseline 82), Na 132 mmol/L, K 4.4 mmol/L, lactate 3.2 mmol/L
data_table.ABG on 4 L NP O2: pH 7.32, PaCO2 32 mmHg, PaO2 62 mmHg, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L
data_table.Background: 78 years, RACF resident, HTN, AF on apixaban, MCI

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily and admit to a monitored bed with intravenous fluid resuscitation and consider intensive care review
options.rationale: Severe CAP (CURB-65 5) is treated with third-generation cephalosporin plus macrolide per eTG; ICU review is indicated for severity. (Source: eTG: Community-acquired Pneumonia)

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.2 g four times daily plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily and admit to the general ward for intravenous fluid resuscitation and monitoring
options.rationale: Benzylpenicillin alone is used for non-severe CAP; severe CAP requires broader gram-negative and atypical cover with ceftriaxone plus macrolide. (Source: eTG: Community-acquired Pneumonia)

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily and admit to the general ward for observation and intravenous fluid resuscitation as per unit protocol
options.rationale: Oral therapy is unsafe in severe CAP (poor bioavailability with vomiting, delayed serum levels); IV route is mandatory. (Source: eTG: Community-acquired Pneumonia)

options.text: Intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g every 8 hours plus intravenous vancomycin 25 mg per kilogram loading dose and admit to the general ward for intravenous fluid resuscitation
options.rationale: Piperacillin-tazobactam plus vancomycin is empirical for HAP/HCAP with MRSA and Pseudomonas concern; CAP does not typically require this cover. (Source: eTG: Community-acquired Pneumonia)

options.text: Intravenous moxifloxacin 400 mg once daily monotherapy and admit to the general ward for intravenous fluid resuscitation and observation as per unit protocol for severe pneumonia care
options.rationale: Respiratory fluoroquinolone monotherapy is reserved for beta-lactam allergy; combination beta-lactam plus macrolide is preferred first line. (Source: eTG: Community-acquired Pneumonia)

explanation.summary: Community-acquired pneumonia severity is stratified with CURB-65 or SMART-COP. CURB-65: Confusion, Urea above 7 mmol/L, Respiratory rate 30 or above, SBP below 90 or DBP 60 or below, age 65 or older; each scores 1. CURB-65 0-1 = mild (outpatient), 2 = moderate (hospital admission), 3 or more = severe (ICU consideration). Empirical antibiotic per Therapeutic Guidelines Australia: mild CAP - amoxicillin 1 g orally 8 hourly plus doxycycline 100 mg orally 12 hourly. Moderate CAP - benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV 6 hourly plus doxycycline 100 mg orally 12 hourly. Severe CAP - ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily (or moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily monotherapy in penicillin anaphylaxis). Directed therapy is guided by sputum culture, blood cultures, urinary pneumococcal and legionella antigens. Adjunctive measures: oxygen to target SpO2 92 percent or above (88 to 92 percent if hypercapnic risk), fluid resuscitation, DVT prophylaxis, review of anticoagulation, sepsis bundle if septic.
key_points: CURB-65 3 or more is severe CAP requiring IV combination and ICU consideration.
Severe CAP: ceftriaxone plus azithromycin per eTG Australia.
Fluoroquinolone monotherapy for penicillin anaphylaxis only.
explanation.pearls: Severe CAP with CURB-65 5: give ceftriaxone 2 g IV plus azithromycin 500 mg IV and consider ICU - not benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline (that is for moderate CAP), and not oral therapy at any severity above mild.

subtopic_detail: Reversal of warfarin anticoagulation in life threatening haemorrhage with a high international normalised ratio
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to the emergency department to assess a 74 year old man brought in by ambulance with two hours of large volume haematemesis and one episode of melaena. He takes warfarin 5 mg daily for atrial fibrillation and his target INR is 2 to 3. He is otherwise well with hypertension on perindopril and ischaemic heart disease. His last INR one week ago was 2.4. He started clarithromycin four days ago for a lower respiratory tract infection.

On assessment he has pulse rate 128 per minute, blood pressure 92/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 per minute, oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air, temperature 36.5 degC. He is pale, diaphoretic and alert. Abdomen is soft with epigastric tenderness. Rectal examination confirms melaena. Investigations: haemoglobin 78 g/L (baseline 138 g/L), platelet count 240 x10^9/L, INR 8.5, activated partial thromboplastin time 42 seconds, fibrinogen 3.2 g/L, urea 22 mmol/L, creatinine 118 micromol/L. Group and hold and cross match for four units of packed red cells have been sent. Two large-bore intravenous cannulas are placed and 500 mL Hartmann has been given. Gastroenterology has been notified for urgent gastroscopy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 128 /min, blood pressure 92/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 /min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.5 degC
data_table.Bleeding: Large volume haematemesis 2 h, one episode of melaena, pale diaphoretic
data_table.Bloods: Hb 78 g/L (baseline 138), platelets 240 x10^9/L, INR 8.5, aPTT 42 sec, fibrinogen 3.2 g/L, urea 22 mmol/L, creatinine 118 micromol/L
data_table.Given so far: 500 mL Hartmann, cross match 4 units RBCs sent
data_table.Medications: Warfarin 5 mg daily for AF, last INR 2.4 one week ago, clarithromycin started 4 days ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate warfarin reversal?

options.text: Intravenous vitamin K 10 mg over 30 minutes and fresh frozen plasma 15 mL per kilogram intravenously as first-line reversal with recheck INR at 2 hours before further intervention
options.rationale: FFP is inferior to PCC in warfarin reversal: slower reversal, higher volume load (dangerous in elderly), higher transfusion reaction risk. (Source: ASTH ASBT Guidelines Warfarin Reversal)

options.text: Oral vitamin K 5 mg single dose and fresh frozen plasma 15 mL per kilogram intravenously as first-line reversal with recheck INR at 2 hours before further intervention
options.rationale: Oral vitamin K is too slow (12-24 h) for life-threatening bleeding; FFP is inferior to PCC (slower, larger volumes, more transfusion reactions). (Source: ASTH ASBT Guidelines Warfarin Reversal)

options.text: Intravenous vitamin K 10 mg over 30 minutes and prothrombin complex concentrate 50 units per kilogram intravenously with cross matched packed red cells transfusion as required
options.rationale: Life-threatening warfarin bleeding at INR 8.5 requires PCC 50 U/kg IV plus IV vitamin K 10 mg per Australasian Society of Blood Transfusion guideline. (Source: ASTH ASBT Guidelines Warfarin Reversal)

options.text: Intravenous vitamin K 1 mg over 30 minutes and cryoprecipitate 10 units intravenously as first-line reversal with recheck INR at 2 hours before further intervention
options.rationale: Cryoprecipitate replaces fibrinogen (already 3.2 g/L in this patient); it does not correct vitamin K-dependent factor deficiency. (Source: ASTH ASBT Guidelines Warfarin Reversal)

options.text: Intravenous idarucizumab 5 g single dose and packed red cell transfusion as required with recheck INR at 2 hours after the idarucizumab and further transfusion as clinically indicated
options.rationale: Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran, not warfarin; irrelevant in a warfarin-treated patient. (Source: ASTH ASBT Guidelines Warfarin Reversal)

explanation.summary: Warfarin bleeding reversal is graded by INR and clinical severity. Life-threatening bleeding at any INR requires prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) 25 to 50 U/kg IV plus vitamin K 5 to 10 mg IV. PCC contains factors II, VII, IX and X and reverses INR within 15 to 30 minutes; vitamin K provides sustained reversal over 6 to 12 hours. Fresh frozen plasma is inferior (slower reversal, larger volume, more transfusion reactions) and used only if PCC unavailable. Non-life-threatening bleeding at INR 4.5 to 10 with warfarin: hold warfarin, oral or IV vitamin K depending on urgency. No bleeding at INR above 4.5 to 10: hold one or two warfarin doses and consider oral vitamin K 1 mg. INR above 10 no bleeding: oral vitamin K 3 to 5 mg and recheck INR. Common precipitants of unexpected INR rise: macrolide antibiotics (clarithromycin, erythromycin), other CYP inhibitors (fluconazole, metronidazole, sulfonamides), amiodarone, dietary changes, liver dysfunction. Cross-match packed red cells for volume replacement is separate from reversal.
key_points: Life-threatening warfarin bleed at any INR: PCC 25-50 U/kg IV plus vitamin K 5-10 mg IV.
PCC preferred over FFP (faster, lower volume, fewer reactions).
Macrolides (clarithromycin) potentiate warfarin via CYP3A4 inhibition.
explanation.pearls: Life-threatening warfarin bleed at INR 8.5: prothrombin complex concentrate 50 U/kg IV plus IV vitamin K 10 mg is standard - FFP is inferior on speed, volume and transfusion reactions.

subtopic_detail: Reperfusion strategy in massive pulmonary embolism when systemic thrombolysis carries elevated bleeding risk
stem:
You are the medical registrar in the emergency department resuscitation bay with a 64 year old woman who collapsed at home two hours ago with sudden onset shortness of breath. She had a right middle cerebral artery ischaemic stroke six months ago with residual mild left arm weakness and no residual dysphasia. She takes apixaban 5 mg twice daily for secondary stroke prevention and has been fully adherent to therapy.

On arrival she is diaphoretic. Pulse rate 128 per minute, blood pressure 82/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 per minute, oxygen saturation 88 percent on 15 L per minute non-rebreather, temperature 36.2 degC, capillary refill 4 seconds. Jugular venous pressure is elevated 6 cm above sternal angle with a loud second heart sound. Bedside echocardiography demonstrates a dilated right ventricle with septal bowing into the left ventricle, McConnell sign, and preserved left ventricular function. Computed tomography pulmonary angiogram shows a large saddle embolus with bilateral proximal pulmonary artery clot and right ventricular to left ventricular diameter ratio 1.6. Troponin 260 ng/L (below 14), lactate 4.2 mmol/L, creatinine 108 micromol/L. She has been given 500 mL Hartmann fluid resuscitation and noradrenaline peripheral is being commenced. Interventional radiology has been contacted to attend within 30 minutes.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 128 /min, blood pressure 82/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 /min, SpO2 88% on 15 L NR mask, temperature 36.2 degC, capillary refill 4 sec
data_table.Cardiovascular: JVP 6 cm above sternal angle, loud P2, diaphoretic
data_table.Echocardiogram: Dilated RV, septal bowing into LV, McConnell sign, preserved LV function
data_table.CT pulmonary angiogram: Large saddle embolus with bilateral proximal pulmonary artery clot, RV/LV ratio 1.6
data_table.Bloods: Troponin 260 ng/L (<14), lactate 4.2 mmol/L, creatinine 108 micromol/L
data_table.Given so far: 500 mL Hartmann fluid, noradrenaline peripheral commencing
data_table.History: Right MCA ischaemic stroke 6 months ago (residual mild L arm weakness), on apixaban 5 mg BD

lead_in: What is the most appropriate reperfusion strategy?

options.text: Urgent catheter-directed thrombolysis via interventional radiology with alteplase infusion into the pulmonary arteries at a reduced dose and unfractionated heparin infusion adjunctive
options.rationale: Catheter-directed thrombolysis is preferred over systemic thrombolysis in massive PE with relative bleeding contraindications (recent ischaemic stroke <3 months absolute, 3-6 months relative). (Source: eTG: Pulmonary Embolism)

options.text: Systemic thrombolysis with intravenous alteplase 100 mg over 2 hours and unfractionated heparin infusion adjunctive with intensive care admission and observation post lysis for 24 hours
options.rationale: Systemic full-dose alteplase risks intracranial haemorrhage in ischaemic stroke at 6 months (relative contraindication); catheter-directed thrombolysis is preferred. (Source: eTG: Pulmonary Embolism)

options.text: Continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily at current dose with therapeutic unfractionated heparin infusion overlap and intensive care admission with reassessment at 6 hours for further intervention
options.rationale: Anticoagulation alone is inadequate in haemodynamically unstable massive PE - reperfusion is required to reduce short-term mortality. (Source: eTG: Pulmonary Embolism)

options.text: Immediate inferior vena cava filter placement without any thrombolysis and continued therapeutic apixaban at current dose with intensive care admission and observation as an isolated strategy
options.rationale: IVC filter alone does not lyse existing clot or improve right ventricular function; it is adjunctive to anticoagulation or reperfusion, not a substitute. (Source: eTG: Pulmonary Embolism)

options.text: Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation cannulation without any thrombolysis or catheter intervention with continued therapeutic apixaban at current dose and intensive care unit admission
options.rationale: ECMO is a bridging strategy for refractory cardiogenic shock from massive PE while reperfusion is arranged; it does not replace the need for thrombolysis or thrombectomy. (Source: eTG: Pulmonary Embolism)

explanation.summary: Pulmonary embolism severity is graded by haemodynamics and RV dysfunction. Massive (high-risk) PE: sustained hypotension below 90 mmHg or need for vasopressors, has 30-day mortality of 25 to 65 percent. Submassive (intermediate-risk): haemodynamically stable with RV dysfunction on echocardiogram or CT (RV/LV ratio above 0.9) and elevated troponin or BNP; 30-day mortality is 3 to 15 percent. Non-massive: neither, mortality below 3 percent. Massive PE mandates urgent reperfusion; systemic thrombolysis (alteplase 100 mg over 2 hours) is first line unless contraindications. Absolute contraindications: haemorrhagic stroke ever, ischaemic stroke within 3 months, active bleeding, intracranial pathology. Relative contraindications: ischaemic stroke 3 to 6 months ago, recent major surgery, uncontrolled hypertension. When systemic lysis is contraindicated or fails, catheter-directed thrombolysis (lower dose alteplase, 20 to 25 mg over 12 to 24 hours via pulmonary artery catheter) or surgical embolectomy is used. ECMO is a bridge for refractory cardiogenic shock. All get anticoagulation.
key_points: Massive PE (SBP below 90) requires urgent reperfusion.
Systemic thrombolysis is first line unless contraindicated by recent stroke or active bleeding.
Catheter-directed thrombolysis or embolectomy when systemic lysis is contraindicated.
explanation.pearls: Massive PE with recent ischaemic stroke at 6 months is a relative contraindication to systemic thrombolysis: catheter-directed thrombolysis with lower-dose alteplase via pulmonary artery catheter is preferred over full-dose IV alteplase.

subtopic_detail: Escalation of care in acute severe asthma refractory to standard nebulised salbutamol ipratropium magnesium and steroid therapy
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar reviewing a 28 year old woman who presented 90 minutes ago with acute severe asthma. She has a background of severe asthma with two intensive care admissions and one intubation in the last five years and takes inhaled fluticasone-salmeterol and montelukast daily. She last used her preventer three weeks ago because she ran out.

On presentation she was speaking in single words with pulse rate 138 per minute, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 34 per minute, oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air, temperature 37.0 degC. She has received back-to-back nebulised salbutamol 5 mg with ipratropium 500 microgram three times, intravenous hydrocortisone 200 mg and intravenous magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 minutes. Ninety minutes into treatment she has pulse rate 148 per minute, blood pressure 108/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 36 per minute, oxygen saturation 91 percent on 6 L per minute nasal prongs, and is now speaking in words to short phrases with improving but still marked accessory muscle use. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.30, PaCO2 48 mmHg, PaO2 68 mmHg, bicarbonate 22 mmol/L, lactate 4.2 mmol/L. Peak expiratory flow rate 130 L per minute (previous best 420 L per minute). Chest examination reveals reduced air entry bilaterally with quiet wheeze; there is no crepitation and no focal signs suggesting pneumonia or pneumothorax.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 148 /min, blood pressure 108/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 36 /min, SpO2 91% on 6 L NP O2, temperature 37.0 degC
data_table.Work of breathing and speech: Words to short phrases, marked accessory muscle use, reduced air entry bilaterally with quiet wheeze
data_table.Peak expiratory flow rate: 130 L/min (previous best 420 L/min, 31 percent of best)
data_table.ABG: pH 7.30, PaCO2 48 mmHg, PaO2 68 mmHg, bicarbonate 22 mmol/L, lactate 4.2 mmol/L
data_table.Given so far (90 min): Salbutamol 5 mg + ipratropium 500 microgram nebs x3, hydrocortisone 200 mg IV, magnesium sulfate 2 g IV over 20 min
data_table.History: Severe asthma, 2 ICU admissions, 1 intubation in 5 years, on fluticasone-salmeterol and montelukast, no preventer 3 weeks

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform bedside chest X-ray to exclude pneumothorax and continue nebulised salbutamol with ipratropium hourly with reassessment of arterial blood gas at 60 minutes further therapy
options.rationale: Imaging is appropriate but does not change immediate management need to escalate bronchodilator therapy and admit to ICU; the two are not mutually exclusive but escalation must not be delayed. (Source: TSANZ Acute Asthma in Adults Guidelines)
source_refs: TSANZ Acute Asthma in Adults Guidelines

options.text: Repeat intravenous magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 minutes and continue nebulised salbutamol with ipratropium hourly on the ward with reassessment of arterial blood gas at 60 minutes further
options.rationale: Repeat MgSO4 has minimal additional benefit after a single 2 g dose; escalation to IV bronchodilator infusion and ICU is indicated with rising PaCO2. (Source: TSANZ Acute Asthma in Adults Guidelines)
source_refs: TSANZ Acute Asthma in Adults Guidelines

options.text: Intravenous aminophylline loading dose 5 mg per kilogram over 20 minutes then infusion 0.5 mg per kilogram per hour with continuous cardiac monitoring and admit to the general ward for observation
options.rationale: Aminophylline has narrow therapeutic window with high toxicity risk in tachycardic hypoxic patient; not routinely recommended in Australian guidelines. (Source: TSANZ Acute Asthma in Adults Guidelines)
source_refs: TSANZ Acute Asthma in Adults Guidelines

options.text: Intramuscular adrenaline 0.5 mg single dose and continue nebulised salbutamol with ipratropium hourly on the ward with reassessment of arterial blood gas at 60 minutes further
options.rationale: IM adrenaline is used in anaphylaxis and severe asthma unresponsive to nebulised beta-agonist without IV access; here IV access exists and IV salbutamol is preferred. (Source: TSANZ Acute Asthma in Adults Guidelines)
source_refs: TSANZ Acute Asthma in Adults Guidelines

options.text: Start intravenous salbutamol infusion 5 microgram per kilogram per minute after loading dose of 200 microgram over 10 minutes with continuous cardiac monitoring and admit to intensive care
options.rationale: Life-threatening asthma with rising PaCO2 refractory to standard therapy escalates to IV salbutamol per TSANZ/eTG with ICU admission. (Source: TSANZ Acute Asthma in Adults Guidelines)
source_refs: TSANZ Acute Asthma in Adults Guidelines

explanation.summary: Acute severe asthma is graded by clinical features and PEFR: severe (PEFR 33 to 50 percent of best, RR >=25, HR >=110, inability to complete sentences) and life-threatening (PEFR below 33 percent of best, silent chest, cyanosis, exhaustion, poor respiratory effort, altered consciousness, arrhythmia, hypotension, SpO2 below 92 percent). Near-fatal features include rising or normal PaCO2 (indicating exhaustion), respiratory acidosis or need for mechanical ventilation. Initial management for severe or life-threatening: oxygen to target SpO2 93 to 95 percent, back-to-back nebulised salbutamol 5 mg and ipratropium 500 microgram every 20 minutes, prednisolone 50 mg orally or hydrocortisone 100 mg IV, IV magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 minutes. Failure to improve or rising PaCO2 escalates to IV salbutamol loading 200 microgram over 10 min then infusion 5 microgram/kg/min in ICU. Non-invasive ventilation is controversial - most guidelines recommend intubation for exhaustion or failure of IV bronchodilator, with ketamine or propofol induction and permissive hypercapnia. Aminophylline is largely superseded and rarely used.
key_points: Life-threatening features: silent chest, exhaustion, cyanosis, altered mental state, rising PaCO2.
IV salbutamol infusion after failure of nebulised beta-agonist plus magnesium.
Aminophylline is not routinely recommended in current Australian guidelines.
explanation.pearls: Severe asthma refractory to nebulised salbutamol, ipratropium, steroid and IV magnesium 2 g with rising PaCO2 to 48 mmHg: escalate to IV salbutamol infusion 5 microgram/kg/min in ICU - not repeat magnesium and not aminophylline.

sources.label: TSANZ Acute Asthma in Adults Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone from cerebral salt wasting after subarachnoid haemorrhage
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 62 year old woman on day 6 of admission for subarachnoid haemorrhage after a Fisher grade 3 bleed from a right posterior communicating artery aneurysm now coiled. She has been on maintenance normal saline 100 mL per hour and nimodipine per protocol. She takes no other medications and has no other medical history.

This morning nursing staff report increased postural dizziness and one episode of confusion overnight. On assessment she has pulse rate 108 per minute, blood pressure 108/62 mmHg supine and 88/54 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 16 per minute, oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degC. Mucous membranes are dry with reduced skin turgor. Fluid balance chart shows negative balance of 2.4 L over the last 24 hours with urine output 3.8 L in 24 hours. She has not been thirsty. Investigations: sodium 122 mmol/L (yesterday 132), potassium 3.6 mmol/L, urea 8.4 mmol/L, creatinine 108 micromol/L (baseline 62), serum osmolality 260 mOsm/kg, urine sodium 88 mmol/L, urine osmolality 480 mOsm/kg, uric acid 0.14 mmol/L. Cortisol and thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits. Chest examination unremarkable and no lower limb oedema.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 108 /min, BP 108/62 supine and 88/54 standing, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Volume status: Dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, negative balance 2.4 L over 24 h, urine output 3.8 L/24 h, not thirsty
data_table.Bloods: Na 122 mmol/L (from 132 yesterday), K 3.6 mmol/L, urea 8.4 mmol/L, creatinine 108 micromol/L (baseline 62), serum osmolality 260 mOsm/kg
data_table.Other: Uric acid 0.14 mmol/L, cortisol and TSH within normal limits, no oedema
data_table.Background: Day 6 post SAH Fisher 3 (posterior communicating aneurysm coiled), maintenance normal saline 100 mL/h, nimodipine

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Intravenous demeclocycline 300 mg twice daily and continue current normal saline 100 mL per hour with daily sodium monitoring and reassessment of fluid balance in 24 hours after commencement
options.rationale: Demeclocycline is a chronic SIADH agent (impairs renal response to ADH); does not correct hypovolaemic CSW and has slow onset. (Source: eTG: Hyponatraemia)

options.text: Fluid restriction to 800 mL per 24 hours and oral sodium chloride tablets 1 g four times daily with daily sodium and osmolality monitoring for the next 72 hours before further intervention
options.rationale: Fluid restriction is treatment for SIADH (euvolaemic), not CSW (hypovolaemic); volume restriction worsens hypovolaemia and cerebral perfusion post SAH. (Source: eTG: Hyponatraemia)

options.text: Oral tolvaptan 15 mg once daily and continue current normal saline 100 mL per hour with daily sodium monitoring and reassessment of fluid balance in 24 hours after tolvaptan commenced
options.rationale: Tolvaptan is a V2 receptor antagonist for SIADH; contraindicated in hypovolaemic hyponatraemia as it worsens hypovolaemia. (Source: eTG: Hyponatraemia)

options.text: Intravenous 3 percent saline 100 mL bolus and then 0.9 percent saline maintenance titrated to maintain positive fluid balance and hourly urine output above 100 mL per hour
options.rationale: Cerebral salt wasting (hypovolaemic hyponatraemia, natriuresis, negative balance post SAH) is treated with volume and sodium replacement, unlike SIADH which restricts fluid. (Source: eTG: Hyponatraemia)

options.text: Rapid intravenous 5 percent dextrose 250 mL per hour to correct sodium urgently and hourly urine output monitoring with target sodium correction of 20 mmol per L over 24 hours as first line
options.rationale: Rapid correction with dextrose worsens hyponatraemia (free water); target correction is 6-8 mmol/L/24 h to avoid osmotic demyelination. (Source: eTG: Hyponatraemia)

explanation.summary: Hyponatraemia after subarachnoid haemorrhage is commonly cerebral salt wasting (CSW) or syndrome of inappropriate ADH (SIADH); distinguishing is critical because treatment is opposite. Volume status is the key discriminator: SIADH is euvolaemic (normal skin turgor, moist mucous membranes, JVP visible), CSW is hypovolaemic (dry mucous membranes, postural drop, tachycardia, negative fluid balance, elevated urea to creatinine). Both feature low serum sodium, elevated urine sodium (above 40 mmol/L), elevated urine osmolality. Uric acid is low in both but a persistently low fractional excretion in SIADH after correction, versus persistently high in CSW, can help retrospectively. Timing: SIADH typically day 4 to 10 post SAH, CSW earlier (day 2 to 7). Treatment: SIADH - fluid restriction 800 to 1000 mL/day, consider salt tabs and, if severe, tolvaptan or demeclocycline. CSW - restore volume with normal saline or hypertonic saline if severe symptomatic; salt replacement. Symptomatic severe hyponatraemia (sodium below 125 with seizures or coma): 3 percent saline 100 mL bolus, repeat up to three times, target sodium rise of 4 to 6 mmol/L acutely then 6 to 8 mmol/L per 24 hours to avoid osmotic demyelination.
key_points: SIADH is euvolaemic; CSW is hypovolaemic - clinical volume status distinguishes them.
SIADH: fluid restrict, tolvaptan; CSW: volume and sodium replacement with saline.
Correct sodium by 6-8 mmol/L per 24 hours to avoid osmotic demyelination.
explanation.pearls: Post-SAH hyponatraemia with postural drop and negative fluid balance is cerebral salt wasting: give 3 percent saline 100 mL bolus and normal saline resuscitation - fluid restriction (SIADH treatment) is the wrong answer.

subtopic_detail: Timing of noradrenaline commencement in septic shock during ongoing fluid resuscitation
stem:
You are the medical registrar in the emergency department resuscitation bay with a 68 year old man with septic shock secondary to community-acquired pneumonia. He has a background of hypertension on perindopril and chronic kidney disease stage 3 with a baseline creatinine of 148 micromol/L. He presented one hour ago and has received empirical intravenous ceftriaxone and azithromycin and 30 mL per kilogram (2 L) of Hartmann solution over the last 45 minutes.

On reassessment he has pulse rate 128 per minute, blood pressure 78/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 per minute, oxygen saturation 92 percent on 6 L per minute nasal prong oxygen, temperature 38.9 degC. His mental state is drowsy but rousable to voice with capillary refill 4 seconds and cool peripheries. Urinary catheter has drained 40 mL in the last hour. Investigations: haemoglobin 128 g/L, white cell count 22.4 x10^9/L, platelet count 148 x10^9/L, urea 22 mmol/L, creatinine 240 micromol/L, lactate 4.8 mmol/L (initial 3.2), bicarbonate 18 mmol/L. Bedside echocardiography shows a hyperdynamic left ventricle with underfilled chambers and no valvular pathology, and an inferior vena cava diameter 1.4 cm with more than 50 percent respiratory variation. A femoral central venous catheter is being placed.
